items.body:
## 1.1 Haemodynamic foundations (supports every topic in this set)

Every cardiac output monitor, fluid strategy and echo finding in this set is an application of five ideas:

- Cardiac output is the product of heart rate and stroke volume.
- Stroke volume depends on preload, afterload and contractility.
- Cardiac output and venous return are the same flow viewed from two ends.
- Oxygen delivery is cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content.
- Fluid responsiveness is a property of the Frank-Starling relationship, not of a pressure number.

### 1.1.1 The core equations

| Variable | Formula | Normal adult values |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiac output (CO) | HR × SV | 4–8 L/min |
| Cardiac index (CI) | CO ÷ BSA | 2.5–4.0 L/min/m² |
| Stroke volume (SV) | CO ÷ HR (or EDV − ESV) | 60–100 mL |
| Stroke volume index (SVI) | SV ÷ BSA | 33–47 mL/m² |
| Mean arterial pressure (MAP) | (CO × SVR ÷ 80) + CVP when SVR is in dyn·s·cm⁻⁵; ≈ DBP + ⅓ pulse pressure at normal heart rates | 70–105 mmHg |
| Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) | SVR = 80 × (MAP − CVP)/CO; SVRI = 80 × (MAP − CVP)/CI | 800–1200 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ |
| Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) | 80 × (mPAP − PAOP) ÷ CO | Approximately 0.5–2 Wood units (40–160 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵); PVR >2 WU is elevated in current PH haemodynamic definitions |
| Ejection fraction (EF) | SV ÷ EDV | 55–70% |

> **Note:** reference ranges vary slightly between textbooks. Know one set, state them as approximate, and show you understand the units (the factor of 80 converts Wood units to dyn·s·cm⁻⁵).

> **Pitfall:** MAP is not a measure of flow. A normal MAP with a low CO and high SVR is a compensated shock state. This is why pressure alone cannot guide resuscitation and why this whole set exists.

### 1.1.2 Determinants of stroke volume

| Determinant | Definition | Clinical surrogates | What changes it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preload | Myocardial fibre length (sarcomere stretch) at end-diastole; ventricular wall stress just before contraction | EDV, LVEDA (echo), PAOP, CVP, GEDV (indicator dilution) | Venous return, blood volume, venous tone, intrathoracic pressure, atrial kick, ventricular compliance |
| Afterload | Wall stress during ejection (Laplace: pressure × radius ÷ (2 × wall thickness)) | SVR, arterial elastance, systolic wall stress | Vascular tone, aortic stenosis, arterial compliance, ventricular dilatation |
| Contractility | Intrinsic myocardial performance at a given preload, afterload and heart rate | EF, dP/dt max, S′ and GLS are load-dependent indices; end-systolic pressure–volume relations are relatively less load-dependent | Sympathetic tone, inotropes, ischaemia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia, negative inotropes (volatiles, β-blockers) |

> **Examiner favourite:** state that CVP and PAOP are pressures and are surrogates for preload (which is a volume or stretch). Compliance links the two, and compliance changes in sepsis, ischaemia, LVH, tamponade and with positive pressure ventilation.

### 1.1.3 Frank-Starling and what it means at the bedside

Stroke volume rises with preload along the ascending limb of the Starling curve and then plateaus. A patient on the ascending limb is **fluid responsive** (SV increases by roughly 10–15% after a fluid challenge of about 500 mL, or after a passive leg raise); a patient on the plateau is not, and further fluid raises filling pressures and tissue oedema without improving flow.

- About half of patients in selected ICU/theatre fluid-challenge studies respond, but prevalence depends on selection and prior treatment. This is not a patient-specific probability, and non-response is not equivalent to proving that all empirical resuscitation was inappropriate.
- The curve shifts with contractility: a failing ventricle has a flatter curve, so the same preload buys less stroke volume and the plateau is reached sooner.
- Fluid responsiveness is **not** the same as fluid need. A responsive patient may still be adequately perfused; the decision to give fluid depends on evidence of inadequate perfusion and on risk of harm from extra fluid.

> **Viva line:** "Fluid responsiveness describes where the patient sits on the Starling curve. It does not tell me they need fluid; it tells me fluid will increase stroke volume if I decide to give it."

![Starling curve and Guyton framework (schematic, not to scale)](set10-fig1.png)

On the steep part of the Starling curve (A) fluid raises stroke volume; on the plateau (B) it does not, and a failing ventricle plateaus sooner. In the Guyton view, fluid shifts the venous return curve to the right and moves the operating point to a higher cardiac output.

### 1.1.4 Venous return and the Guyton framework

In steady state, cardiac output equals venous return. Venous return is driven by the gradient between mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf) and right atrial pressure, divided by the resistance to venous return:

VR = (Pmsf − PRA) ÷ RVR, where Pmsf is mean systemic filling pressure, PRA is right atrial pressure and RVR is the resistance to venous return.

- Pmsf is determined by **stressed volume** (the part of blood volume that distends vessel walls, about 25–30% of the total) and venous compliance. Venodilation (anaesthetic agents, neuraxial block) converts stressed to unstressed volume and lowers Pmsf.
- The heart sets the right atrial pressure (a heart with better function lowers PRA and increases venous return); the vasculature sets Pmsf and RVR.
- Cardiac output is where the cardiac function curve intersects the venous return curve. Fluid shifts the venous return curve to the right (raises Pmsf); vasopressors raise Pmsf by venoconstriction; inotropes shift the cardiac function curve.
- Positive pressure ventilation and PEEP raise right atrial and intrathoracic pressures, reducing the gradient for venous return.

### 1.1.5 Oxygen delivery and consumption

DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ × 10

CaO₂ (mL O₂/dL) = (1.34 × Hb in g/dL × SaO₂ as a fraction) + (0.003 × PaO₂ in mmHg)

NZ units: when Hb is in g/L, calculate CaO₂ in mL O₂/L as 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.225 × PaO₂ in kPa, then DO₂ = CO in L/min × CaO₂ in mL/L. Do not add an extra factor of 10 in that unit system.

| Variable | Typical resting value |
|---|---|
| DO₂ | about 1000 mL/min (500–600 mL/min/m²) |
| VO₂ | about 250 mL/min (110–160 mL/min/m²) |
| Oxygen extraction ratio (VO₂ ÷ DO₂) | about 25% |
| SvO₂ (true mixed venous, PA blood) | about 65–75% |
| ScvO₂ (SVC blood) | usually slightly lower than SvO₂ in health; reversed in shock |

- When DO₂ falls, the extraction ratio rises to preserve VO₂.
- Below a critical DO₂, which varies with physiology and disease rather than one universal extraction threshold, VO₂ becomes supply-dependent, anaerobic metabolism begins and lactate rises.
- Three of the four determinants of DO₂ (CO, Hb, SaO₂) are the targets of resuscitation, and CO is the one that monitoring in this set is designed to measure.

### 1.1.6 Static versus dynamic assessment of preload

| Type | Examples | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Static pressure | CVP, PAOP | Easily measured | Poor predictors of fluid responsiveness in most studies; affected by compliance, valvular disease, intrathoracic pressure |
| Static volume | LVEDA (echo), GEDV, RVEDV | Closer to actual preload | Still a single point on the curve; does not show the slope |
| Dynamic (heart–lung interaction) | PPV, SVV, IVC and SVC variation | Predict responsiveness well when valid | Require controlled ventilation, tidal volume about 8 mL/kg predicted body weight, sinus rhythm, closed chest, no right heart failure or raised intra-abdominal pressure |
| Dynamic (functional challenge) | Passive leg raise, fluid challenge, end-expiratory occlusion test | Work in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia (PLR) | Need a real-time flow measure (not BP alone) to read the response |

> **Examiner favourite:** the reason dynamic indices work is that positive pressure inspiration reduces RV preload and increases RV afterload; the effect on LV stroke volume appears a few beats later. A patient on the steep part of the Starling curve shows large respiratory variation; a patient on the plateau does not.

> **Pitfall:** none of the cardiac output monitors in the following sections tells you what to do. They tell you what the circulation is doing. The decision still needs a clinical question: is perfusion inadequate, and is a fluid, vasopressor, inotrope or source control the right answer?

## 1.2 Estimating cardiac output and choosing a monitor

No clinical sign estimates cardiac output reliably, so every quantitative method rests on one of five principles: Fick, indicator dilution, Doppler, arterial waveform analysis or electrical impedance/bioreactance. Each has a characteristic failure mode, and the exam answer is largely about stating that failure mode and matching the monitor to the patient.

### 1.2.1 Properties of an ideal cardiac output monitor

- Accurate, precise and reproducible, with a response time fast enough to detect clinically relevant change.
- Continuous or near-continuous, and able to track trends even if absolute values are imperfect.
- Non-invasive or minimally invasive, operator-independent, safe, cheap and usable in awake and anaesthetised patients.
- Ideally also provides preload and fluid responsiveness data, because CO alone does not diagnose hypovolaemia.

No available device meets all of these. Thiele et al. (Crit Care Med 2015) concluded that thermodilution and Doppler techniques have acceptable accuracy against experimental reference standards, whereas bioimpedance, pulse contour, partial rebreathing and pulse wave velocity devices are less well validated and mostly show lower accuracy.

### 1.2.2 Clinical estimation

Examination (capillary refill, skin temperature, mottling, mental state), urine output, blood pressure and lactate give a qualitative picture of perfusion. Cardiac output cannot be reliably inferred from them: a normal blood pressure is compatible with a very low cardiac index and high SVR. Use them as the clinical context for any number a device gives you.

### 1.2.3 Fick principle

Oxygen uptake by the lungs equals the arteriovenous oxygen content difference multiplied by flow.

CO (L/min) = VO₂ (mL/min) ÷ [10 × (CaO₂ − CvO₂) in mL/dL]; omit ×10 if content is in mL/L

- **Direct Fick (oxygen):** needs measured VO₂ (respiratory gas analysis), arterial and true mixed venous blood (PA sample). Historically the reference standard but impractical; assuming a VO₂ (for example 125 mL/min/m²) introduces large errors, particularly in critical illness.
- **Partial CO₂ rebreathing (NICO):** applies the Fick principle to CO₂ using a brief rebreathing loop; the change in end-tidal CO₂ and CO₂ elimination gives non-shunted pulmonary capillary flow, and a shunt correction estimates total CO.
  - Needs controlled ventilation and stable ventilation and is inaccurate with significant shunt or V/Q mismatch.

### 1.2.4 Indicator dilution

A known amount of indicator injected upstream is measured downstream; the area under the concentration-time curve is inversely proportional to flow (Stewart-Hamilton).

CO = amount of indicator ÷ area under the concentration-time curve (∫ c(t) dt)

| Method | Indicator and sites | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pulmonary artery thermodilution | Cold fluid via PAC right atrial port; thermistor at PA tip | The clinical reference standard; intermittent bolus or continuous (heating filament) |
| Transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO, EV1000/VolumeView) | Cold injectate via central vein; thermistor in a large artery (femoral or axillary) | Also yields GEDV, extravascular lung water, cardiac function index; used to calibrate pulse contour |
| Lithium dilution (LiDCO) | Small IV lithium chloride bolus (peripheral vein); lithium-selective electrode on arterial line | Avoid in patients on lithium; non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers can interfere with the sensor; calibrates a pulse power algorithm |
| Dye dilution (indocyanine green) | Dye via vein; pulse dye densitometry | Mainly historical and research use |

**Pitfall (PAC thermodilution):**

- The technique assumes all flow passes through the right heart in a mixed stream.
- It is unreliable with significant tricuspid regurgitation, intracardiac shunts and in very low-flow states.
- Technique errors (injectate volume and temperature, speed of injection, timing in the respiratory cycle) are common; the usual practice is to average several measurements within a tolerance.

### 1.2.5 Doppler techniques

Doppler measures blood velocity; flow = velocity × cross-sectional area.

SV = VTI × CSA (velocity time integral × cross-sectional area), and **CO = SV × HR**

- Oesophageal Doppler (e.g. CardioQ): probe in the lower oesophagus measures descending thoracic aortic velocity; area is estimated from a nomogram (age, height, weight) and a fixed fraction of CO (roughly 70%) is assumed to pass down the descending aorta.
  - Provides SV, corrected flow time (FTc, a preload index; roughly 330–360 ms normal) and peak velocity (a contractility index).
  - Limits: probe position dependence, usually requires an anaesthetised or suitably sedated, cooperative patient, oesophageal pathology and varices, aortic disease, and changes in the proportion of CO to the descending aorta (aortic cross-clamping, severe vasoconstriction).
- **Echocardiographic Doppler:** SV from LVOT velocity time integral × LVOT area (see topic 2).

### 1.2.6 Bioimpedance and bioreactance

Thoracic impedance changes with each ejection of blood (bioimpedance) or the phase shift of an applied current changes (bioreactance, e.g. NICOM). Completely non-invasive, but affected by arrhythmia, electrical interference (diathermy), lung water, pleural effusion and movement. Evidence of accuracy is weaker than for thermodilution.

### 1.2.7 Arterial waveform analysis

Pulse contour (calibrated or uncalibrated) and volume-clamp (finger cuff) systems estimate SV from the arterial waveform. These are covered in subsection 1.5 with their limitations.

### 1.2.8 Judging a monitor: accuracy versus trending

- Bland-Altman analysis gives bias (mean difference) and limits of agreement (±1.96 SD) against the reference method.
- Percentage error (approximately 1.96 × SD of paired differences ÷ mean reference CO × 100%) below about 30% is a historical acceptability benchmark, derived assuming sufficient precision of the reference method (Critchley and Critchley, 1999).
  - Joosten et al.
  - (BJA 2017) used this criterion in their meta-analysis of non-invasive devices.
- Trending ability (four-quadrant and polar plots, concordance rate) is assessed separately. A device may trend better than its absolute agreement, but both the direction and size of change must be reliable enough to distinguish a clinically meaningful response from measurement noise.

> **Examiner favourite:** a monitor that is "validated" in stable patients may not be accurate in vasoplegia, rapidly changing vascular tone or arrhythmia. Say which populations the evidence covers.

### 1.2.9 Comparison of methods

| Method | Invasiveness | Outputs | Main strengths | Main limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PAC thermodilution | Invasive (central, right heart) | CO, PA pressures, PAOP, SvO₂ | Reference standard; pressures and SvO₂ | Complications, expertise, TR/shunt errors, intermittent |
| Transpulmonary thermodilution | Minimally invasive (CVC + arterial thermistor) | CO, GEDV, EVLW, SVV, CFI | Calibration of pulse contour; EVLW | Needs special arterial line; intermittent calibration |
| Lithium dilution | Minimally invasive | CO, calibrates PulseCO | Peripheral injection; no CVC | Lithium therapy, NMB interference, calibration |
| Uncalibrated pulse contour | Minimally invasive (arterial line) | CO, SV, SVV, PPV | Simple, fast to set up | Unreliable with changing vascular tone, arrhythmia, damping |
| Oesophageal Doppler | Minimally invasive (oesophageal probe) | SV, FTc, peak velocity | Evidence base in GDT; real-time | Usually anaesthetised/sedated; operator-dependent; assumed aortic fraction |
| Echocardiography (TTE/TOE) | Non-invasive / semi-invasive | SV, EF, valve and structural data | Explains why haemodynamics are abnormal | Operator-dependent, intermittent, training required |
| Bioimpedance / bioreactance | Non-invasive | CO, SV | Needs no access | Artefact-prone, variable accuracy |
| Finger-cuff volume clamp | Non-invasive | BP, CO, SVV | Continuous, no cannula | Vasoconstriction, oedema, limited validation in shock |
| Partial CO₂ rebreathing | Minimally invasive (ventilator circuit) | CO | Non-vascular | Shunt, ventilation changes, controlled ventilation only |

### 1.2.10 Choosing a monitor to guide fluid management (BT_GS 1.77)

Start with the question being asked, then match the monitor to the patient and the operation.

- What is the question? (Is flow low? Is this patient fluid responsive? Why is this patient unstable?) A device that tracks stroke volume answers the first two; echo answers the third.
- **Patient factors:** ventilated or spontaneously breathing, sinus rhythm or AF, cardiac disease, right heart failure, vasoplegia, contraindications (oesophageal disease, lithium, coagulopathy).
- **Surgical factors:** major abdominal, vascular, orthopaedic or emergency surgery with large fluid shifts; expected duration and blood loss; positioning; cross-clamping.
- **Practical factors:** access already in place (an arterial line may allow pulse contour), local expertise, cost and consumables.
- **Evidence:** benefit in perioperative trials comes from a protocol linked to the monitor, typically stroke volume optimisation, not from the device itself (see goal-directed therapy, topic 6).

| Clinical scenario | Reasonable first choices |
|---|---|
| Major elective abdominal surgery, ventilated, sinus rhythm | Oesophageal Doppler or arterial pulse contour with SVV/PPV, in a GDT protocol |
| High-risk patient with existing arterial line | Pulse contour (calibrated if haemodynamically labile) |
| Awake, spontaneously breathing or arrhythmic | Passive leg raise with a real-time flow measure; echo |
| Cardiac surgery or severe cardiac dysfunction | TOE; PAC where PA pressures or right heart function matter |
| Shock of uncertain cause | Echocardiography first, then device-based monitoring |
| Pulmonary oedema or ARDS with shock | Transpulmonary thermodilution (EVLW) or PAC |

**Guidance note:** NICE medical technology guidance MTG3 (2011) supported oesophageal Doppler monitoring (CardioQ-ODM) in major or high-risk surgery. It has since been replaced by the cardiac output monitoring recommendations in the NICE perioperative care in adults guideline (NG180, 2020).

### 1.2.11 Intensive care patient: cardiac output and fluid optimisation (SS_IC 1.28)

- **Use a stepwise approach:** clinical assessment and bedside echo first
  - Dynamic tests selected for the conditions: PLR or a measured fluid challenge can be used during spontaneous breathing or arrhythmia
  - End-expiratory occlusion requires controlled ventilation and a sustained occlusion without respiratory effort
  - Add an arterial-line-based or transpulmonary thermodilution system when ongoing monitoring is needed.
- **Pulse contour accuracy is limited during haemodynamic instability.** A meta-analysis comparing pulse contour systems with PAC thermodilution concluded that agreement during instability was limited; prefer calibrated systems or confirm with echo if the clinical picture does not fit the number.
- Transpulmonary thermodilution gives EVLW and GEDV, helpful when the risk of pulmonary oedema constrains fluid therapy.
- **Fluid is a drug:** the four-phase model (resuscitation, optimisation, stabilisation, evacuation) frames when fluid helps and when removal is the aim. Fluid responsiveness testing should be repeated, not assumed from the last result.

**SAQ frame for "Evaluate means of estimating CO":** (1) classify by invasiveness and principle; (2) for each state the principle, one advantage and one limitation; (3) state how accuracy is judged (bias, percentage error, trending); (4) finish with how you would choose for a specific patient.

## 1.3 Central venous pressure

Central venous pressure is a poor predictor of fluid responsiveness and should not be used alone to decide whether to give fluid. Its remaining value is as a trend, as a marker of right heart function and venous congestion, and as a safety limit, not as a target.

### 1.3.1 What is measured and how

- **Definition:** pressure in the superior vena cava or right atrium relative to atmosphere, from a central venous catheter with the tip at the cavo-atrial junction (lower SVC).
- **Reference point:** zero the transducer at the level of the right atrium (phlebostatic axis: fourth intercostal space, mid-axillary line, supine). A 1 cm height error is about 0.7 mmHg.
- **Normal value:** about 0–8 mmHg (roughly 2–10 cmH₂O). Convert: 1 mmHg = 1.36 cmH₂O.
- Read at end-expiration, when intrathoracic pressure is closest to atmospheric. In a spontaneously breathing patient this is the highest point of the trace; in a ventilated patient the lowest.
- **Check the system:** square wave test, no air bubbles, and tip position confirmed by an appropriate validated method; a venous waveform alone does not localise the tip.

### 1.3.2 What determines the CVP

| Raises CVP | Lowers CVP |
|---|---|
| Hypervolaemia, venoconstriction | Hypovolaemia, venodilation (GA, neuraxial block, sepsis) |
| RV failure, pulmonary hypertension, PE | Vigorous inspiratory effort (spontaneous breathing) |
| Tricuspid stenosis or regurgitation | Standing or head-up position |
| Tamponade, constrictive pericarditis |  |
| PEEP, positive-pressure ventilation, raised intra-abdominal pressure |  |
| Increased intrathoracic pressure (tension pneumothorax, asthma) |  |

CVP is therefore the net result of venous return and the heart's ability to handle it. A high CVP can mean too much volume or a heart that cannot cope with normal volume.

### 1.3.3 The CVP waveform

| Component | Event | Abnormalities |
|---|---|---|
| a wave | Atrial contraction (follows P wave) | Absent in AF; large regular a waves with tricuspid stenosis, PH or reduced RV compliance; cannon a waves when atrial contraction meets a closed tricuspid valve (e.g. AV dissociation) |
| c wave | Tricuspid valve bulging into the RA at the start of ventricular systole | Often not visible |
| x descent | Atrial relaxation and downward movement of the tricuspid annulus | Lost or flattened in tricuspid regurgitation |
| v wave | Passive atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve | Large (giant v) in tricuspid regurgitation |
| y descent | Tricuspid opening and RA emptying | Steep in constrictive pericarditis and severe TR; slow or absent in tamponade and tricuspid stenosis |

> **Examiner favourite:** Kussmaul's sign (a paradoxical rise in CVP with inspiration) suggests constriction, restrictive cardiomyopathy or RV infarction.

### 1.3.4 Evidence: why CVP fails as a guide to fluids

- Systematic reviews of studies that compared CVP with the response to a fluid challenge found a very poor relationship between CVP and blood volume, and CVP predicted fluid responsiveness barely better than chance (summary AUC 0.56, 95% CI 0.54–0.58, across 43 studies in Marik and Cavallazzi's 2013 meta-analysis, with a pooled correlation of only 0.18 between baseline CVP and the change in stroke or cardiac index, and about 57% of patients being fluid responders).
  - Their earlier 2008 review found a pooled correlation of 0.16 between CVP and measured blood volume.
- The reasons are physiological: venous capacitance and compliance vary widely between patients and over time, intrathoracic pressure shifts the number, and the relationship between preload and stroke volume depends on contractility (the Starling curve is not the same for any two patients).
- The early goal-directed therapy trial (Rivers, 2001) used a CVP target of 8–12 mmHg. The later trials (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe) did not show a benefit of protocolised EGDT with CVP targets over usual care, and the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 guideline favours dynamic measures (passive leg raise or fluid bolus response) over static parameters to guide fluid.
- A high CVP is not neutral. Elevated venous pressure reduces organ perfusion pressure (organ perfusion pressure = MAP − venous pressure) and is associated with venous congestion and acute kidney injury.

### 1.3.5 Where CVP still has a role

- **Trend and response to a fluid challenge:** interpret the rise alongside measured SV/CO and congestion. The classical Weil stop rule (>5 cmH₂O rise after 200 mL) is historical teaching, not a validated universal modern fluid algorithm; pressure change alone cannot establish response.
- **Right heart assessment:** a persistently high CVP with low cardiac output points to RV failure, pulmonary hypertension, tamponade or tricuspid disease and should prompt echocardiography.
- **Safety limit:** an upper limit to avoid venous congestion, particularly in AKI, liver disease or after transplant.
- **Waveform diagnosis:** AF, AV dissociation, tricuspid regurgitation, tamponade.
- **Access, not measurement:** most central lines are placed for vasopressor administration, long-term access or irritant drugs, with CVP as a by-product.

### 1.3.6 Practical points in the perioperative setting

- Positive-pressure ventilation, PEEP, pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg all move CVP independent of volume status. Interpret relative to the patient's own baseline in the same conditions.
- A CVP of 3 mmHg in a ventilated patient is not the same as 3 mmHg in a spontaneously breathing one.
- Do not insert a central line solely to measure CVP. The risk-benefit does not support it as a perioperative fluid guide.

> **Viva line:** "CVP is a pressure, not a volume. It reflects the interaction between venous return and cardiac function, so it cannot tell me where the patient is on the Starling curve. I would use dynamic measures such as passive leg raise or pulse pressure variation, and I would use CVP for trend, congestion and right heart diagnosis."

**SAQ frame for "Evaluate the place of CVP":** (1) what it measures and normal range; (2) determinants and waveform; (3) why it fails to predict fluid responsiveness (physiology and evidence); (4) where it still adds value; (5) what you would use instead.

## 1.4 Pulmonary artery catheter (role and data P2; insertion and waveforms P5)

The PAC remains the reference standard for intermittent cardiac output and the only widely available way to measure pulmonary artery pressures, PAOP and SvO₂ together, but randomised trials have shown no outcome benefit in unselected patients. The exam answer is a balanced one: what it measures, how to interpret the numbers, and the small group in whom it still helps.

### 1.4.1 The catheter

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Size and length | Usually 7–7.5 Fr, 110 cm, marked every 10 cm; passed through an 8.5–9 Fr introducer |
| Distal lumen (yellow) | At the tip; PA pressure, PAOP, mixed venous sampling |
| Proximal lumen (blue) | About 30 cm from the tip, sits in the right atrium; CVP, injectate port for thermodilution |
| Balloon lumen | Inflated with up to 1.5 mL air (not liquid, not CO₂ for long-term due to diffusion) to flow-direct the catheter and obtain the wedge |
| Thermistor | About 4 cm from the tip; measures PA blood temperature |
| Variants | Continuous CO (heating filament), continuous SvO₂ (fibreoptic), RVEF, pacing ports |

### 1.4.2 Insertion technique (P5)

**Indications and contraindications:**

- See subsection 1.4.8.
- Relative contraindications include LBBB (risk of complete heart block if RBBB develops), a biological tricuspid/pulmonary prosthesis (specialist assessment), right heart thrombus or tumour, and severe coagulopathy.
- A mechanical tricuspid or pulmonary valve must not be traversed.
- Experienced operators and appropriate monitoring are essential.

- **Prepare:** consent, full monitoring including ECG and defibrillator available, full aseptic barrier precautions, ultrasound-guided access to the right internal jugular vein (shortest, most direct path to the right heart).
- **Check the catheter:** test the balloon (it should inflate symmetrically and deflate fully), flush all lumens, connect the distal port to a pressure transducer, zero and level at the phlebostatic axis, use a sterile sleeve.
- Advance with the balloon deflated through the introducer to about 15–20 cm, then **inflate the balloon** and advance with pressure waveform monitoring.
- **Recognise the sequence of waveforms:** RA (about 15–25 cm via the right IJ) → RV (about 25–35 cm; watch for ventricular ectopy) → PA (about 35–45 cm) → wedge (about 45–55 cm).
  - Distances are approximate and longer from the left IJ, subclavian or femoral routes; rely on the waveform change rather than the distance, and follow the catheter's own markings.
- Obtain the wedge, deflate the balloon, confirm the PA trace returns, and record the final position (usually 45–55 cm from the right IJ). A wedge trace appearing with less than the full balloon volume suggests the tip is too distal: withdraw.
- **Secure and confirm:** chest X-ray (tip in a proximal PA, usually within approximately 2 cm of the hilum, without peripheral migration; West zone 3 physiology is required for reliable PAOP), sterile sleeve, record the insertion depth.
- **Ongoing care:** inflate only for brief wedge readings (never leave the balloon inflated), continuous PA trace, regular review of the need for the catheter, avoid advancing a catheter that has been withdrawn through the sleeve.

> **Pitfall:** the most dangerous mistakes are leaving the balloon inflated in the wedge position (pulmonary infarction, PA rupture), over-inflating, and flushing against a wedged catheter.

### 1.4.3 The pressure waveforms (P5)

| Site | What you see | Typical values (mmHg) |
|---|---|---|
| Right atrium | a, c, v waves as for CVP | Mean 0–8 |
| Right ventricle | Rapid systolic upstroke, then diastolic with small a-wave rise at end; no dicrotic notch; diastolic pressure near zero | 15–30 / 0–8 |
| Pulmonary artery | Systolic peak, dicrotic notch (pulmonary valve closure), diastolic runoff; diastolic baseline higher than the RV | 15–30 / 4–12; mean 9–18 |
| Wedge (PAOP) | Damped left atrial trace with a and v waves, delayed relative to the ECG; mean usually ≤PA diastolic; exceptions include large v waves | Mean 6–12 |

![PAC insertion via the right internal jugular vein (schematic, not to scale)](set10-fig2.png)

Traces are schematic. Depths are approximate for a right internal jugular approach and should be checked against the manufacturer's guide.

**Examiner favourite:**

- How do you confirm a true wedge?
- Waveform changes from PA to atrial type with a and v waves, with an appropriate delay; PAOP is usually no higher than PA diastolic pressure, but large v waves or other pathology can alter this.
- If uncertain, cautious distal wedge blood sampling by an experienced operator should approach systemic arterial saturation.
- A true wedge normally retains respiratory variation; absence of variation may indicate overwedging.
- Confirm an appropriate non-distal PA position and West zone 3 conditions; a CXR alone cannot prove a valid wedge.

### 1.4.4 Measured and derived variables (P2)

| Variable | How obtained | Use |
|---|---|---|
| CO, CI | Thermodilution (bolus or continuous) | Global flow |
| PA pressures, mean PAP | Direct | Pulmonary hypertension; RV afterload |
| PAOP | Wedge | Estimate of left atrial pressure (and LVEDP when valid) |
| SvO₂ | Distal port sample or fibreoptic | Global balance of delivery and extraction |
| SVR, SVRI | SVR = 80 × (MAP − CVP)/CO; SVRI = 80 × (MAP − CVP)/CI | Vascular tone |
| PVR | 80 × (mPAP − PAOP) ÷ CO | Pulmonary vascular disease |
| Transpulmonary gradient and diastolic pulmonary gradient | mPAP − PAOP; PADP − PAOP | Characterisation alongside mPAP, PAOP and PVR; neither gradient alone defines pre/postcapillary PH |
| DO₂, VO₂ | CO × CaO₂; CO × (CaO₂ − CvO₂); apply ×10 if O₂ content is in mL/dL and CO in L/min | Oxygen supply and extraction |

### 1.4.5 Interpreting the data: a method

- **Check validity first:** zero and level correct, damping optimal (square wave test), waveform appropriate, thermodilution curve smooth, measurements repeated and consistent.
- **Read the flow:** is the cardiac index low (below about 2.2 L/min/m²)? Is SvO₂ low (below about 60–65%), suggesting high extraction?
- **Read the filling pressures:** CVP and PAOP, remembering they are surrogates.
- **Read the resistance:** SVR and PVR.
- Assign a pattern and cross-check with the patient, echo and the clinical story.

| Pattern | CVP | PAOP | CI | SVR | SvO₂ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypovolaemic | Low | Low | Low | High | Low |  |
| Cardiogenic (LV failure) | Normal or high | High | Low | High | Low |  |
| Septic / vasodilatory | Low or normal | Low or normal | High, normal or low at any stage | Low | Normal or high (impaired extraction) |  |
| Obstructive: massive PE | High | Normal or low | Low | High | Low | High PVR; PA pressure may be only modestly raised in profound RV failure |
| Tamponade | High | High | Low | High | Low | Equalisation of diastolic pressures (RA, RVEDP, PADP, PAOP) |
| RV infarction | High | Low or normal | Low | High | Low | CVP greater than PAOP |
| Pulmonary hypertension (pre-capillary) | High | Normal | Low | Normal or high | Low | High PVR and transpulmonary gradient |
| Acute mitral regurgitation | Normal | High with giant v wave | Low | High | Low | PAOP trace shows large v waves |

**Worked example:**

- BP 80/40, HR 120, CVP 14, PA 45/28 (mean 34), PAOP 24, CI 1.7, BSA 2.0 m² (CO 3.4 L/min), SvO₂ 52%, calculated SVR approximately 925 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵.
- Flow is low, filling pressures are high, SVR is within the usual range despite hypotension, and extraction is high: cardiogenic shock with raised left-sided filling pressure.
- Next steps are echocardiography for the cause (infarct, acute MR, VSD), then inotrope, afterload and revascularisation decisions.

### 1.4.6 Limitations of the PAOP

- PAOP reflects left atrial pressure, which can approximate end-diastolic LV pressure when pulmonary venous/mitral transmission and timing are appropriate; mean LA pressure is a different physiological quantity from LVEDP.
- It **overestimates** LVEDP in mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation (large v waves), raised intrathoracic pressure and pulmonary venous obstruction; it **underestimates** LVEDP in severe aortic regurgitation (premature mitral valve closure) and with a stiff, non-compliant LV.
- High PEEP and West zone 1 or 2 positioning may make PAOP reflect alveolar rather than left atrial pressure.
- Even a correct PAOP remains a pressure surrogate for preload.

### 1.4.7 Complications

| Category | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Access | Pneumothorax, arterial puncture, haematoma, air embolism | Ultrasound reduces these |
| Arrhythmia | Ventricular ectopy (common), VT/VF, RBBB (complete heart block if pre-existing LBBB), atrial arrhythmia | Withdraw to RA if persistent |
| Catheter-related | Knotting, balloon rupture (latex allergy), valve damage, entrapment in cardiac structures | Do not force |
| Pulmonary | Pulmonary infarction (persistent wedge), PA rupture (rare, very high mortality: risk factors include age, female sex, pulmonary hypertension, anticoagulation, over-inflation, distal tip) | PA rupture: haemoptysis, position bleeding lung down, protect airway (selective intubation or bronchial blocker), correct coagulopathy, early specialist input |
| Infection | Catheter-related bloodstream infection, endocarditis | Related to duration of use |
| Thrombosis | Catheter-related thrombus, thromboembolism |  |

### 1.4.8 Role and evidence (P2)

Observational data (SUPPORT, 1996: 5735 critically ill adults, 30-day mortality odds ratio about 1.24 with PAC use) suggested harm; the randomised trials that followed found no routine outcome benefit, with catheter-related harms in several studies:

| Trial | Population | Main finding |
|---|---|---|
| Sandham (NEJM 2003) | Elderly high-risk surgical patients | No mortality benefit; more pulmonary emboli with PAC |
| PAC-Man (Lancet 2005) | ICU patients | No difference in hospital mortality (68% versus 66%, adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.94–1.27) in over 1000 patients from 65 UK ICUs |
| ESCAPE (JAMA 2005) | Advanced heart failure | No difference in days alive out of hospital |
| FACTT (NEJM 2006) | Acute lung injury | No benefit of PAC versus CVC-guided therapy; more arrhythmia with PAC |
| Cochrane review (2013) | Multiple critically ill and surgical populations | No difference in mortality or length of stay (13 studies, 5686 patients) |

**Trial evidence:**

- Sandham (NEJM 2003; 1994 high-risk surgical patients) found hospital mortality of about 7.8% with PAC-guided care versus 7.7% with standard care without PAC (a CVC was not mandated), with more pulmonary emboli in the PAC group.
- FACTT (NEJM 2006; 1001 patients with acute lung injury) found 60-day mortality of about 27.4% versus 26.3%, with more catheter-related complications in the PAC group.
- ESCAPE (JAMA 2005; 433 patients with severe heart failure) found days alive and out of hospital of 133 versus 135 (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.82–1.21), 180-day mortality of 10% versus 9%, and more in-hospital adverse events with the PAC (21.9% versus 11.5%), with no PAC-related deaths.
- The Cochrane review by Rajaram (2013) pooled 13 trials and 5686 patients and found no difference in mortality or length of stay.

**Where it still has a role:**

- Right ventricular failure and pulmonary hypertension (diagnosis, response to vasodilators, transplant assessment)
- Cardiac surgery with severe LV or RV dysfunction
- LVAD and heart transplant management
- Selected cardiogenic shock where echo does not resolve the mechanism
- Complex mixed shock
- Situations where continuous SvO₂ and PA pressures change management.
- Observational data in cardiogenic shock suggest benefit from PAC-guided care, but no definitive randomised trial has shown that it improves outcome.

**Why use has fallen:** no outcome benefit in trials; complications; the rise of echo and less-invasive cardiac output monitors; the requirement for expertise to interpret data.

> **Viva line:** "The PAC is a diagnostic tool, not a therapy. Its value depends entirely on the clinician acting on the data correctly, which is why trials of its use in unselected patients are neutral."

**SAQ frame for "Evaluate the role of the PAC":** (1) what it measures; (2) interpretation and limitations of PAOP; (3) complications; (4) trial evidence; (5) selected indications today; (6) alternatives.

## 1.5 Continuous cardiac output monitoring

- Pulse contour and related devices give beat-to-beat stroke volume from an arterial line and allow dynamic fluid-responsiveness indices.
- They are less invasive than a PAC and are the workhorse of perioperative goal-directed therapy, but they rest on assumptions about arterial compliance and impedance that fail when vascular tone is changing, which is exactly when you most want an answer.

### 1.5.1 Principle of pulse contour and pulse power analysis

- The arterial pressure waveform is generated by stroke volume interacting with the compliance and impedance of the arterial tree (Windkessel model). If compliance and impedance are known, stroke volume can be derived from the waveform.
- Pulse contour (for example PiCCO) analyses the area under the systolic part of the waveform and applies a patient-specific calibration factor from transpulmonary thermodilution.
- Pulse power (for example LiDCO) assumes conservation of mass and power: net change in power in the arterial system after each beat is proportional to the net flow. LiDCOplus is calibrated by lithium dilution; LiDCOrapid uses a nominal calibration. Device generation and software matter.
- Uncalibrated waveform systems (FloTrac, ProAQT/Pulsioflex, LiDCOrapid) use device-specific models of the arterial waveform; some incorporate demographics and waveform statistics. Algorithms differ and cannot be treated as interchangeable. Without independent calibration, changing vascular tone can impair accuracy.

> **Examiner favourite:** these devices estimate SV from arterial pressure. When SVR is changing rapidly (vasopressor infusions, vasoplegia, rewarming, aortic clamping) the relationship between the waveform and SV drifts, so the number can be wrong even when the trace looks clean.

### 1.5.2 Types of device

| Device type | Examples | Access | Calibration | Outputs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calibrated: transpulmonary thermodilution | PiCCO, EV1000/VolumeView | Central venous line plus femoral or axillary arterial thermistor line | Cold injectate bolus | CO, SV, SVV, GEDV, EVLW, CFI, SVR |
| Calibrated: lithium dilution | LiDCOplus | Peripheral vein, radial arterial line | Lithium bolus | CO, SV, SVV, PPV, SVR, DO₂ |
| Uncalibrated arterial waveform | FloTrac/Vigileo, ProAQT, LiDCOrapid, MostCare | Standard arterial line | Device-specific model; PRAM/MostCare derives impedance from the waveform | CO, SV, SVV, PPV |
| Volume-clamp finger cuff | ClearSight (Nexfin), CNAP | Finger cuff | Reconstructs brachial waveform | CO, SV, BP, SVV |
| Oesophageal Doppler | CardioQ | Oesophageal probe | Nomogram | SV, FTc, peak velocity |
| Bioreactance | NICOM | Chest electrodes | Phase-shift algorithm | CO, SV |
| Continuous PAC thermodilution | Vigilance | PAC | Filament pulses | Continuous CO (delayed 5–10 min) |

### 1.5.3 Dynamic indices: SVV and PPV

SVV = [(SVmax − SVmin) ÷ SVmean] × 100%

PPV = {(PPmax − PPmin) ÷ [(PPmax + PPmin) ÷ 2]} × 100%

During positive-pressure ventilation, inspiration transiently reduces RV preload and increases RV afterload, and the effect reaches the LV a few beats later. A preload-responsive ventricle shows large cyclic variation in stroke volume and pulse pressure.

- **Thresholds:** PPV above about 13% (Michard 2000) and SVV above about 10–13% predict fluid responsiveness.
  - Cannesson described a "grey zone" of roughly 9–13% where the index is unreliable.
  - In Marik's 2009 systematic review of ventilated patients, the pooled AUCs for predicting fluid responsiveness were 0.94 for PPV, 0.84 for SVV and 0.86 for systolic pressure variation, compared with 0.55 for CVP, 0.56 for GEDVI and 0.64 for LVEDAI.
  - Cut-offs differ between devices and studies, so quote them as approximate.
- **Valid conditions:** controlled mechanical ventilation, tidal volume about 8 mL/kg predicted body weight, sinus rhythm, closed chest, normal intra-abdominal pressure, normal RV function.
- **Invalid or unreliable:** spontaneous breathing, arrhythmias (especially AF), low tidal volume (a brief, supervised 6-to-8 mL/kg predicted-body-weight challenge may improve interpretation), low lung compliance, open chest, high intra-abdominal pressure, RV failure or pulmonary hypertension (false positive), low heart-rate/respiratory-rate ratio (<about 3.6), and high-frequency ventilation.

> **Pitfall:** a low PPV or SVV does not prove the patient is fluid non-responsive if any of the above invalidating conditions are present.

- Functional tests in practice: PLR from a semi-recumbent position to a supine trunk with legs at 45° requires a rapid flow measurement, usually within 30–90 seconds, and return to baseline confirmation.
- Avoid pain or active leg lifting; raised intra-abdominal pressure may cause false negatives.
- End-expiratory occlusion usually lasts about 15 seconds during controlled ventilation; a small CO rise (~5%) requires a sufficiently precise monitor and no spontaneous inspiratory interruption.

### 1.5.4 Strengths and limitations

| Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|
| Less invasive than PAC and continuous | Accuracy limited during haemodynamic instability and changing vascular tone |
| Provide SV and dynamic indices in real time | Dependent on a high-quality arterial waveform (damping, resonance, positioning) |
| Use an existing arterial line (uncalibrated) | Calibrated systems need extra lines or reagents |
| Suitable for goal-directed protocols | Dynamic indices invalid in many real-world conditions |
| Lower complication rates than PAC | Arrhythmia, aortic regurgitation, IABP and aortic pathology degrade accuracy |
|  | Cost; expertise; outcome benefit depends on the protocol, not the device |

Systematic reviews comparing pulse contour devices against thermodilution have found only limited agreement during haemodynamic instability, and trending ability varies by device and software version. Meta-analyses of non-invasive systems (finger cuff, bioreactance) report percentage errors that often exceed the 30% criterion.

### 1.5.5 Role in anaesthesia and ICU

- **Perioperative:** high-risk major surgery where large fluid shifts or haemodynamic instability are expected; used within a stroke-volume optimisation protocol (see topic 6).
- **ICU:** shock with uncertainty about mechanism; titration of vasopressors, inotropes and fluid; EVLW to guide fluid restriction when using transpulmonary thermodilution.
- **Not a substitute for echo:** these devices report a number; they do not diagnose tamponade, severe valvular disease or RV failure.

> **Viva line:** "Pulse contour monitors estimate stroke volume under assumptions about the arterial tree. Accuracy and trending depend on device, calibration, software and patient conditions; rapidly changing vascular tone is a major warning, and I verify a surprising value clinically or with echo."

**SAQ frame for "Evaluate the role of continuous cardiac output devices":** (1) classification; (2) principle and assumptions; (3) dynamic indices and validity conditions; (4) accuracy evidence; (5) where they help in anaesthesia and ICU; (6) limitations and alternatives.

items.title: 2. Focused cardiac ultrasound and echocardiography in haemodynamic instability
items.body:
- Echocardiography is a first-line bedside imaging tool for identifying mechanisms of haemodynamic instability; it complements examination, ECG, lung ultrasound and other investigations.
- Device-based monitors give a number; echo gives a diagnosis (hypovolaemia, LV or RV failure, tamponade, valve lesion, outflow obstruction) that determines whether the answer is fluid, vasopressor, inotrope, drainage or surgery.

## 2.1 Role in perioperative haemodynamic management (AT_GS 1.23)

### Preop

Identify a new symptom, murmur or suspected ventricular/valve disease that would change management; request comprehensive echo when indicated rather than routine screening. Establish baseline function and plan expertise/access for the operation.

| Setting | Role of echo |
|---|---|
| Pre-operative | Focused TTE for unexplained dyspnoea, murmur, suspected LV dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension before higher-risk surgery |
| Intra-operative TOE: cardiac and aortic surgery | Routine: baseline and post-repair assessment, de-airing, RV and LV function, guidance of surgical decisions |
| Intra-operative TOE: non-cardiac surgery | Rescue or diagnostic tool for unexplained, persistent or life-threatening haemodynamic instability (hypovolaemia vs LV/RV failure, tamponade, PE, air embolism, LVOT obstruction); also major vascular, liver transplant, high-risk cardiac patients |
| Post-operative / ICU / emergency | Focused TTE to diagnose shock, assess fluid responsiveness and monitor response |
| Cardiac arrest | Brief, protocolised assessment during rhythm checks for reversible causes (tamponade, massive PE, hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax) without prolonging pauses in compressions |

**Advantages:** immediate, non-invasive (TTE) or semi-invasive (TOE), real-time, repeatable, diagnostic, directly assesses structure, valves and function, and guides treatment.

**Limitations:** operator dependence and training requirement; image quality (obesity, lung disease, surgical dressings); intermittent snapshot rather than a continuous trend; findings change with loading and anaesthetic agents; TOE has its own risks and equipment cost.

- TOE contraindications.
- Oesophageal perforation, major obstructing/structural oesophageal disease and active upper GI bleeding are major contraindications.
- Diverticulum, recent upper-GI surgery, prior radiation, varices, coagulopathy, cervical instability and hiatus hernia need case-specific assessment; classifications differ between guidelines.
- Check the procedure/anatomy and seek specialist advice rather than treating every previous gastric operation as an absolute prohibition.
- Complications include dental injury, bleeding, oesophageal or gastric injury, aspiration and arrhythmia.

**Training and credentialing:**

- ANZCA PG46 (Guideline on training and practice of perioperative echocardiography in adults, June 2025) sets minimum study numbers: basic TOE 100 studies over 24 months, comprehensive TOE or TTE 200, and combined TTE and TOE 240. TOE should be used only when clinically indicated.
- The guideline does not grant credentialing; scope of practice is the responsibility of the employing institution.
- PG47 (Perioperative diagnostic point-of-care ultrasound, April 2025) sets cardiac POCUS training at no fewer than 90 studies and lung at no fewer than 50, and valvular pathology should be referred for comprehensive echocardiography.

### Intraop

Use TOE when indicated for cardiac surgery or persistent unexplained instability, within competency and contraindication limits. Define the mechanism before treating; monitor the response and document findings. Do not prolong CPR interruptions for ultrasound.

### Postop

Use focused TTE for new shock, respiratory deterioration or suspected cardiac complications; compare with baseline and repeat after treatment. Escalate an incomplete or discordant study to comprehensive echo/TOE and appropriate specialist review.

## 2.2 A basic haemodynamic assessment with TTE or TOE (SS_CS 1.24)

Use a fixed, repeatable sequence so that nothing is skipped under pressure. A reasonable order is: pericardium, LV (size and function), RV, valves, IVC and filling status, then flow measurement.

Core views

| Question | TTE view | TOE view |
|---|---|---|
| Global LV function, wall motion, preload | Parasternal short axis (papillary level), apical four-chamber | Transgastric mid short-axis for rapid mid-LV size/function assessment; combine with other views to assess all LV segments, RV and valves, mid-oesophageal four-chamber and two-chamber |
| LV outflow tract, aortic valve, root | Parasternal long axis; apical five-chamber | Mid-oesophageal long axis and aortic valve short axis |
| RV size and function | Apical four-chamber (TAPSE), subcostal | Mid-oesophageal four-chamber, RV inflow-outflow |
| Pericardial effusion | Subcostal, parasternal | Mid-oesophageal four-chamber, transgastric |
| Fluid status | Subcostal IVC | Bicaval view (SVC variation) |
| Stroke volume | Apical five-chamber PW Doppler in LVOT, parasternal long axis for LVOT diameter | Deep transgastric or transgastric long axis for LVOT Doppler |

What to look for

| Domain | Findings and what they suggest |
|---|---|
| LV size and filling | Small, hyperdynamic cavity with end-systolic obliteration ("kissing papillary muscles"): hypovolaemia or vasoplegia. Dilated, globally hypokinetic LV: systolic failure or cardiomyopathy |
| LV function | Qualitative (hyperdynamic, normal, reduced) plus ejection fraction by biplane Simpson's (normal about 55% or higher); fractional area change from the transgastric short axis; regional wall motion abnormality by coronary territory |
| RV | Size relative to LV (RV:LV ratio above about 1 is severe dilatation); TAPSE ≤17 mm or S′ ≤9.5 cm/s are abnormal longitudinal-function indices in ASE 2025 guidance; interpret with RV size, FAC/other indices, load and clinical context; septal flattening (D-shaped LV) shows pressure overload (systolic flattening) or volume overload (diastolic flattening); McConnell's sign (RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing) may support acute RV strain but is not specific for PE (also seen in RV infarction) |
| IVC | In spontaneously breathing adults, diameter and inspiratory collapse estimate right atrial pressure; they do not independently establish fluid responsiveness (below 2.1 cm with more than 50% collapse suggests RAP about 3 mmHg; above 2.1 cm with less than 50% collapse suggests about 15 mmHg) |
| Valves | Colour Doppler for regurgitation, stenosis gradient and calcification; acute severe MR or AR in shock |
| Pericardium | Effusion size and signs of tamponade (see 2.3) |
| Filling pressure | Average E/e′ >14 may support raised LA pressure but is not a stand-alone diagnosis; apply an integrated diastolic assessment, with rhythm and valve-specific limitations (ASE 2025) |
| Pulmonary pressure | RVSP = 4(TR Vmax)² + RAP; approximates PASP only without pulmonary stenosis/RV outflow obstruction and with an adequate Doppler signal |

Key haemodynamic calculations

SV = LVOT VTI × π × (LVOT diameter ÷ 2)², and **CO = SV × HR**

ΔP = 4V² (simplified Bernoulli), and **AVA = (LVOT area × LVOT VTI) ÷ AV VTI** (continuity equation)

- LVOT VTI (apical five-chamber, pulsed-wave Doppler in the LVOT): roughly 18–22 cm is normal; a value below about 15 cm suggests low stroke volume. Reference ranges differ slightly between echo laboratories.
- LVOT diameter (parasternal long axis, mid-systole, about 2 cm): the square in the area formula is the main source of error, so measure carefully and, when assessing change, do not re-measure the diameter.
- **Fluid responsiveness:** a rise in LVOT VTI (or SV) of about 10–15% after passive leg raise or a fluid bolus identifies a responder; respiratory variation of aortic peak velocity of more than about 12% predicts responsiveness in ventilated patients.
- **IVC:** in ventilated patients an IVC distensibility index above roughly 18% predicts responsiveness if tidal volume is adequate and there is no right heart failure or raised intra-abdominal pressure. In spontaneously breathing patients IVC collapsibility is a weaker guide.

> **Pitfall:** a hyperdynamic, empty LV in a hypotensive patient may be hypovolaemia, vasoplegia or dynamic LVOT obstruction. Look for systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and a late-peaking, dagger-shaped LVOT Doppler signal before giving more inotrope.

Fluid tolerance is a separate question: look for worsening RV/LV filling, venous congestion, lung B-lines and impaired oxygenation as fluid is given. VExUS combines hepatic/portal/intrarenal venous Doppler with IVC assessment to describe congestion; it is not a stand-alone volume or fluid-responsiveness test, and outcome-guided treatment thresholds remain uncertain.

## 2.3 Echocardiography in the haemodynamically unstable patient (SS_CS 1.25)

Protocols such as RUSH (rapid ultrasound for shock and hypotension: pump, tank, pipes), FATE and FoCUS give a structured way to combine cardiac, IVC, lung and vascular views.

| Shock type | Echo findings |
|---|---|
| Hypovolaemic | Small, hyperdynamic LV; end-systolic obliteration; small, collapsing IVC; flat or empty RV |
| Cardiogenic | Dilated or globally hypokinetic LV or regional wall motion abnormality; mitral regurgitation; raised E/e′; plethoric IVC; B-lines on lung ultrasound; complications of MI (VSD, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture) |
| Obstructive: pulmonary embolism | Dilated, hypokinetic RV; D-sign; McConnell's sign; TAPSE low; plethoric IVC; sometimes clot in transit; small underfilled LV |
| Obstructive: tamponade | Effusion with RA systolic/RV early-diastolic collapse, venous congestion and exaggerated mitral/tricuspid respiratory variation (roughly >25%/>40% in spontaneous breathing); mechanical ventilation, PH and postoperative loculated collections can alter or obscure these signs |
| Obstructive: tension pneumothorax | Absent sliding alone is nonspecific (also apnoea, mainstem intubation, pleurodesis); use lung pulse/B-lines/lung point and context. With clinical tension physiology, decompress immediately without waiting for imaging |
| Distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis) | Hyperdynamic LV with low SVR; small or normal cavity early; LV/RV dysfunction can coexist from the outset; echo cannot measure low SVR directly without pressure/flow information |
| Aortic dissection | Dilated aortic root, intimal flap, aortic regurgitation, pericardial effusion |
| Dynamic LVOT obstruction | Hyperdynamic LV, SAM of mitral valve, late-peaking LVOT gradient, mitral regurgitation jet |

Practical points

- Treat echo as part of the clinical examination, not a separate investigation. The same finding (a small LV) means different things in different patients.
- Repeat the study after intervention to confirm response.
- In cardiac arrest, image only during planned rhythm checks and do not delay compressions.
  - ANZCOR Guideline 11.6 (April 2025) suggests against routine POCUS during CPR to diagnose reversible causes.
  - It may be considered as a targeted adjunct when it can be done without interfering with standard ALS and a specific reversible cause is suspected, and it should not be used to prognosticate during CPR.
- If images are non-diagnostic or findings conflict with the clinical picture, call for expert assistance and consider TOE.

> **Viva line:** "I would use a focused echo to answer four questions: is the LV empty or full and is it contracting; is the RV dilated; is there fluid around the heart; and is there a major valve lesion or outflow obstruction. That tells me whether to give fluid, a vasopressor, an inotrope, or drain or operate."

**SAQ frame for "Discuss the role of echo in the unstable patient":** (1) why echo (diagnosis, not just a number); (2) a systematic approach; (3) findings by shock type; (4) limitations and pitfalls; (5) risks and competency requirements for TOE.

items.title: 3. Monitoring standards and choosing appropriate perioperative monitoring
items.body:
PG18 sets the minimum monitoring for every anaesthetic and puts clinical observation by a vigilant anaesthetist first; PS55 makes the facility responsible for providing the equipment and staffing to meet it. Know the mandatory items, the ones that are "available" rather than mandatory, and the principle that equipment supplements but never replaces clinical observation.

- The text below follows PG18 (July 2025 version, which carries Appendix 1 of February 2023).
- The learning outcome refers to the earlier PS55 title "Recommendations on Minimum Facilities…"; the current document is a position statement (August 2021) with Appendix 1 (2021), Appendix 2 on dantrolene (2026) and Appendix 3 on fire (2024).
- Appendix 2 requires an initial 720 mg of dantrolene within 5 minutes and a further 480 mg within 1 hour, with 1200 mg stocked if more cannot be obtained within 60 minutes.

## 3.1 PG18 Guideline on monitoring during anaesthesia: principles

- Applies to general anaesthesia, major regional anaesthesia/analgesia and sedation.
- Monitoring fundamental physiological variables is essential; clinical judgement determines how long it continues after anaesthesia.
- The healthcare facility provides and maintains the equipment on the advice of designated specialist anaesthetists (see PS55).
- Recommendations may need to be exceeded depending on pre-anaesthesia assessment.
- Equipment must be used with careful clinical observation, because equipment may not detect unfavourable clinical developments.
- Visual and audible alarms are enabled at the start of anaesthesia and disabled only in exceptional circumstances (for example during cardiopulmonary bypass), then restored as soon as practicable.

## 3.2 Presence and observation

- The vigilant anaesthetist cannot be the practitioner performing the procedure.
- A medical practitioner whose sole responsibility is anaesthesia care must be constantly present from induction until safe transfer to recovery or ICU.
- Brief unavoidable absences require temporary delegation (including recording and a plan for significant perturbations) to a suitably trained and competent practitioner.
- Permanent handover goes to an anaesthetist able to accept continued responsibility (PS53).
- The anaesthetist ensures all necessary equipment is available, including special monitoring (for example MRI) or remote monitoring to protect staff.

## 3.3 What must be monitored and recorded

| Domain | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Circulation | Detect the arterial pulse and supplement with arterial blood pressure; recorded no less often than every 10 minutes; omission of BP must be clinically justifiable |
| Ventilation | Monitored continually |
| Oxygenation | Clinical observation (including adequate lighting for colour) with instrument monitoring |

## 3.4 Monitoring equipment

| Monitor | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Oxygen analyser | Continuous operation, with low-oxygen audible alarm, for every patient when an anaesthesia breathing system is in use |
| Pulse oximeter | In use for every patient undergoing general anaesthesia or sedation, with variable pulse tone and low-threshold alarm audible to the anaesthetist |
| Breathing-system disconnection or ventilator-failure alarm | Continuous operation, automatically activated, whenever an automatic ventilator is in use |
| Carbon dioxide monitor | Quantitative, with continuous display of level and waveform, in use for every patient having general anaesthesia and immediately available for sedation; a sustained capnogram of appropriate morphology and amplitude indicates ventilation |
| ECG | Available for every anaesthetised patient and used for general and major regional anaesthesia as clinically indicated |
| Intermittent non-invasive BP | Available for every patient, with a range of cuff sizes |
| Continuous invasive BP | Equipment available (arterial line and transducer) |
| Brain function monitor | Available when clinically indicated, particularly in patients at high risk of awareness |
| Inhalational agent monitor | In use for every general anaesthetic where volatile agents are delivered (inspired and end-tidal concentration) |
| Temperature | Continuous core temperature monitoring available for every general anaesthetic and used whenever warming devices are in use |
| Neuromuscular function | Quantitative monitoring available for every patient who received neuromuscular blockade and used whenever extubation is considered after non-depolarising blockade |
| Other (when clinically indicated) | EEG, CVP, cerebral oximetry, TOE, cardiac output, respiratory mechanics |

> **Examiner favourite:** capnography is part of confirming correct airway placement as well as ventilation; PG18 cites the consensus guideline on preventing unrecognised oesophageal intubation (Chrimes et al., 2022).

**Recording:** regular observations are documented in the anaesthesia record, manually or electronically (PG06).

- Practical distinction: PG18’s maximum 10-minute interval is a minimum standard, not the preferred NIBP interval for every GA.
- Five-minute cycling is common and shorter intervals or an arterial line are appropriate during instability.
- After non-depolarising block, verify quantitative train-of-four ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; availability of a monitor alone does not establish recovery.

## 3.5 Appendix 1: previous axillary nodal dissection

- The appendix addresses whether an arm that has had axillary node dissection can be used for cannulation and blood pressure monitoring.
- It notes limited and poor evidence to support avoiding the affected arm and recommends shared decision-making.
- Without lymphoedema there is no contraindication to non-invasive BP, cannulation or an arterial line in the affected arm.
- With lymphoedema, an alternative site should be considered where practicable, but there is no absolute contraindication.
- The risks of central venous access or an arterial line are likely to outweigh the benefits if avoiding the arm is the only indication.

## 3.6 PS55 Position statement on minimum facilities

PS55 describes the minimum staffing, equipment, medication and service processes required wherever anaesthesia is administered, including operating suites and other anaesthetising locations (and facilities providing deep sedation).

| Domain | Key points |
|---|---|
| Staffing | A dedicated assistant for the anaesthetist (PS08); adequate help immediately available; credentialled practitioners (PS02) |
| Location | Adequate space, lighting, power and back-up, telecommunications, piped gas or cylinders, scavenging, access to resuscitation and help; special considerations for non-operating room locations, which carry greater risk |
| Equipment | Anaesthesia machine and workstation complying with PS54; breathing systems (including paediatric); ventilation with alarms; suction reserved for the anaesthetist, with a backup; airway equipment including at least two laryngoscopes and a separate difficult airway trolley with a front-of-neck access kit; a separate means of delivering oxygen independent of the anaesthesia system; monitoring per PG18; cardiac defibrillator with synchronised cardioversion; infusion devices; patient warming; transfer devices. Staffing and environment: a dedicated assistant, at least three staff immediately available to position the patient, room temperature 18–28°C, and cognitive aids highly recommended. Complex surgery needs direct arterial and venous pressure measurement, rapid fluid infusion and active warming. |
| Medications and processes | Emergency drugs and drugs for malignant hyperthermia and local anaesthetic toxicity; pre-anaesthesia consultation (PG07); recovery care (PS04); safe medication practices (PG51); infection control (PG28) |
| Fire safety | Appendix 3 (2024) covers prevention and management of non-airway fires in operating suites |

**Viva line:**

- "The core is a vigilant anaesthetist.
- Apply PG18’s specific indications: pulse oximetry and capnography for GA, oxygen analysis when a breathing system is used, agent monitoring when volatile agents are delivered, circulation/BP observations, and ECG as clinically indicated.
- Monitor temperature during active warming and use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring when considering extubation after non-depolarising blockade.
- The facility supplies suitable equipment."

> **SAQ frame:** (1) principle of vigilance and who may monitor; (2) mandatory versus available-when-indicated monitors; (3) frequency of recording; (4) alarm management; (5) facility responsibilities under PS55; (6) circumstances that exceed the minimum.

items.title: 4. Vascular access: shock, peripheral/IO access, CVCs, PICCs, ultrasound and rapid infusion
items.priority: P3 MODERATE overall (5 P3 parent LOs) + P5 site/ultrasound details
items.los: BT_RT 1.35; AT_GS 1.11; AT_GS 1.12; BT_GS 1.71; AR_ME 3.2 (vascular access component); AT_GS 1.14 (P5); AT_GS 1.13 (P5)
items.body:
The common thread is choosing the access that matches the job: flow rate for resuscitation, vein preservation and duration for therapy, and patient comfort for routine cases.

## 4.1 Increasing success and reducing discomfort of peripheral cannulation (BT_GS 1.71)

| Domain | Measures |
|---|---|
| Preparation | Explain the procedure, warm the patient and the limb, hydrate, allow the arm to hang dependent, apply a tourniquet or sphygmomanometer cuff at a pressure between venous and arterial, keep calm |
| Venodilation | Warm packs, gravity, tapping or fist clenching, selected local-policy adjuncts; topical GTN is not routine, and may cause headache or hypotension |
| Site selection | Forearm or dorsum of the hand with a straight, palpable vein; avoid joints, bifurcations, areas of infection or oedema and, where lymphoedema is present, the affected arm (see subsection 3.5); choose the largest suitable vein for the intended cannula |
| Technique | Skin traction to anchor the vein, correct angle (shallow), advance slightly after flashback so the catheter tip is in the lumen, then advance the catheter off the needle; use a cannula size matched to the vein |
| Technology | Ultrasound guidance for difficult access (higher first-pass success); near-infrared vein illumination as an adjunct |
| Reducing pain | Topical local anaesthetic cream (for example EMLA (usually ≥60 minutes on intact skin) or amethocaine (often 30–45 minutes), following age, dose and product instructions; intradermal buffered lidocaine; vapocoolant spray; needle-free jet lidocaine; distraction and play therapy in children; nitrous oxide when available |
| Safety and quality | Aseptic technique, secure fixation, document the date and review daily in line with the ACSQHC Peripheral Intravenous Catheter Clinical Care Standard (remove when no longer needed) |

**Complications:** pain, failed cannulation, haematoma, infiltration and extravasation, phlebitis and thrombophlebitis, arterial puncture or injection, nerve injury, local infection and bloodstream infection.

## 4.2 Vascular access in the shocked patient (BT_RT 1.35)

**Principle:** obtain the fastest reliable access that allows the required flow, without delaying resuscitation or other life-saving treatment. Flow through a rigid tube follows Hagen-Poiseuille:

Q = π r⁴ ΔP ÷ (8 η L) (Hagen-Poiseuille: flow Q, radius r, pressure gradient ΔP, viscosity η, length L)

Flow is proportional to the fourth power of radius and inversely proportional to length. Short, wide cannulae (and shortened tubing) are better than long catheters; pressure bags or pumps increase ΔP; warm, less viscous fluids flow faster.

| Cannula size (gauge) | Approximate gravity flow rate (water) |
|---|---|
| 14 G | about 240–270 mL/min |
| 16 G | about 140–180 mL/min |
| 18 G | about 75–100 mL/min |
| 20 G | about 50–60 mL/min |
| 22 G | about 30–40 mL/min |

**Source of the figures:**

- Approximate gravity-flow rates for water through standard-length peripheral cannulae; manufacturers differ slightly.
- Flow is proportional to the fourth power of the radius and inversely proportional to length (Hagen-Poiseuille), so a short, wide cannula flows faster than a long, narrow one of the same gauge.
- A large-bore introducer (8.5–9 Fr) or rapid infusion catheter in a central vein can exceed the flow through peripheral cannulae.

Stepwise approach

- Two large-bore peripheral IV cannulae (14–16 G) in the forearm or antecubital fossa; the external jugular vein is an option.
- Ultrasound-guided peripheral access if landmark attempts fail.
- Intraosseous access early rather than late (proximal humerus, proximal tibia, distal tibia).
  - It allows fluids, blood, drugs and vasopressors.
  - Contraindications: fracture or recent IO attempt in the same bone, infection over the site, prosthesis, osteogenesis imperfecta.
  - Complications: extravasation and compartment syndrome, osteomyelitis, fat embolism, pain on infusion.
- Central access: femoral (rapid, compressible, away from the airway and chest) or internal jugular with a large-bore introducer, preferably under ultrasound; the subclavian vein is less favourable when coagulopathic.
- Venous cut-down at the saphenous vein at the ankle as a last resort.
- Neonates: umbilical vein.

> **Pitfall:** do not use central access with a long, narrow catheter as the primary resuscitation line; a short large-bore peripheral line gives better flow.

**IV or IO in cardiac arrest:** ANZCOR Guideline 11.2 (June 2024) suggests IV access as the preferred route for drug delivery during cardiac arrest; if IV attempts are unsuccessful or not feasible, use IO access (weak recommendation, very low certainty evidence).

Peripheral noradrenaline can bridge to central access under a protocol: use a reliable, visible proximal vein and an appropriate catheter, verify patency, inspect frequently and have an extravasation response plan. It should not delay central access when prolonged or escalating support is needed.

## 4.3 PICC lines (AT_GS 1.11, AT_GS 1.12)

**What a PICC is:** a long catheter (usually 3–6 Fr, single, double or triple lumen) inserted through a peripheral arm vein, with the tip at the cavo-atrial junction (lower SVC).

**Indications:** medium-term intravenous therapy (weeks to months): chemotherapy, parenteral nutrition, prolonged antibiotics, irritant or vesicant infusions, and difficult peripheral access.

**Contraindications and cautions:** local infection, thrombosis in the target vein, coagulopathy (relative), chronic kidney disease stage 3b or worse where vein preservation for dialysis access is needed, ipsilateral axillary dissection or lymphoedema, and ipsilateral pacemaker or defibrillator leads.

**Anatomy:**

- The basilic vein (medial) is preferred, in the mid-upper arm (the zone with the largest veins and least risk to the brachial artery and median nerve)
- The brachial veins are paired with the artery and median nerve
- The cephalic vein is a less preferred option because of its tortuosity.
- The brachial artery and median nerve lie close to the basilic and brachial veins.

Insertion technique (ultrasound-guided modified Seldinger)

- Consent; measure the external length (insertion site to the sternal notch, then to the third intercostal space on the right) to estimate catheter length.
- Position the patient supine with the arm abducted at 90° and the tourniquet applied.
- Full aseptic technique with maximal barrier precautions (sterile gown, gloves, drape, mask, cap) and chlorhexidine skin preparation.
- Ultrasound identification of the vein (compressible, no pulsation) and nearby artery and nerve; local anaesthetic.
- Micro-introducer needle puncture, guidewire insertion, small skin incision, then peel-away introducer.
- Advance the catheter to the measured length; turning the head towards the ipsilateral shoulder or flexing the chin reduces the chance of misdirection into the internal jugular vein.
- **Confirm tip position:** intracavitary ECG (maximal P wave at the cavo-atrial junction), fluoroscopy or chest X-ray.
- Aspirate, flush, secure with a securement device, apply a sterile dressing, and document length and indication.

**Complications:** malposition (IJ vein, contralateral veins, right atrium or ventricle with arrhythmia), upper limb deep vein thrombosis, phlebitis, catheter-related bloodstream infection, catheter occlusion, fracture or embolisation, air embolism, bleeding, nerve injury, arterial puncture.

PICC versus CVC

Device selection also includes midlines and long peripheral cannulae: a midline tip remains peripheral and must not be assumed suitable for all central-only infusions. Select the fewest necessary lumens, preserve future dialysis veins, and follow device-specific power-injection limits.

| Feature | PICC | CVC (non-tunnelled) |
|---|---|---|
| Typical duration | Weeks to months | Days to weeks |
| Insertion | Arm vein, can be done by trained nurses at bedside | Neck, chest or groin; requires a trained operator |
| Immediate procedural risk | Lower (no pneumothorax, less arterial puncture and haemothorax) | Higher (pneumothorax, haemothorax, carotid puncture) |
| Thrombosis | Higher rates of upper limb DVT in hospitalised patients (Chopra, Lancet 2013: odds ratio 2.55, 95% CI 1.54 to 4.23, in 11 comparative studies; number needed to harm about 26; about 14% in critically ill patients in single-arm studies) | Lower DVT rates in comparison but subclavian and IJ thrombosis occur |
| Infection | Do not infer infection outcomes from Chopra’s 2013 VTE review; PICCs are not reliably infection-sparing in hospitalised patients | Related to site, number of lumens, care bundle and duration; no universal site ranking applies to all patients |
| Flow rate | Low (long, narrow lumen); poor for rapid resuscitation | Depends on lumen/length: standard multilumen CVCs are not rapid-infusion devices; a dedicated wide-bore introducer is different |
| Pressure measurement and sampling | CVP possible but damped; sampling more prone to occlusion | Reliable CVP and sampling |
| Vein preservation | Compromises arm veins used for future fistula | Also requires preservation of central veins, particularly avoiding subclavian stenosis in future dialysis patients |
| Patient comfort and mobility | Good for long-term use and outpatients | Lower |
| Use in anaesthesia | Poor for rapid resuscitation; CVP can be measured through a suitable patent PICC if system dynamics and position are validated | Suited for vasopressors, large-volume resuscitation, CVP |

## 4.4 Central venous cannulation: indications and contraindications

- Central venous cannulation gives reliable access for vasopressors and irritant infusions, pressure monitoring and large-volume resuscitation.
- Route choice trades infection and thrombosis risk against mechanical complications (subsection 4.5); ultrasound guidance has become the standard of care for internal jugular cannulation and reduces failure and complications (subsection 4.7).

**Indications:** vasopressor or irritant infusion; difficult peripheral access; CVP or ScvO₂ monitoring when it will change management; large-bore access for resuscitation; parenteral nutrition; renal replacement or plasmapheresis (dialysis catheters); transvenous pacing; PAC introducer; aspiration of venous air embolism.

**Contraindications (relative):** local infection or anatomical distortion at the site, coagulopathy (particularly for subclavian puncture), SVC obstruction or thrombosis, uncooperative patient, and absence of a clear indication.

## 4.5 Routes compared

| Route | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| Right internal jugular | Straight, short path to the SVC and right atrium; compressible; ultrasound-friendly; site risk depends on patient and care conditions | Carotid puncture; pneumothorax (less than subclavian); patient discomfort and dressing difficulty; access to head blocked in neurosurgery |
| Left internal jugular | Usable when the right is not | Longer, more angled path; risk of vessel or pleural injury; thoracic duct injury |
| External jugular | Superficial, low procedural risk | Often difficult to advance the guidewire to the central circulation; high failure rate |
| Subclavian | Lowest catheter infection and thrombosis rates in comparative trials; comfortable for the patient; stable dressing | Highest pneumothorax risk; non-compressible bleeding; subclavian artery puncture; harder under ultrasound; stenosis risk for future dialysis access |
| Femoral | Quick, easy, compressible, away from airway and chest; useful in cardiac arrest and trauma | Infection/thrombosis concerns, but risk varies with patient, site care and duration; hip flexion; femoral artery puncture; retroperitoneal haematoma; DVT |

**Examiner favourite:**

- The ANZICS Central Line Insertion and Maintenance Guideline (2012, endorsed by the ANZICS Safety and Quality Committee) is a bundle: surgical scrub with chlorhexidine for the proceduralist, maximal barrier precautions (cap, mask, eye protection, sterile gown and gloves, full-body drape), skin preparation with at least 0.5% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol allowed to dry, clipping rather than shaving, site chosen on clinical grounds (it prefers the subclavian vein in most patients), and daily review of whether the line is still needed.
- This historical bundle should now be read alongside PG28 infection-control guidance and the 2025 safe vascular-access guideline; real-time ultrasound is recommended for central access, not just elective IJ cannulation.

Site selection summary: individualise the route to urgency, anatomy, bleeding/mechanical risk, infection risk, future dialysis access, surgical field and operator competence.
