Right IJ is often convenient; ultrasound-guided axillary/subclavian or femoral access may be preferable in a particular patient. Do not delay emergency access to satisfy a rigid site hierarchy.

## 4.6 Basic technique (Seldinger, ultrasound-guided right IJ)

- Consent, checklist and time-out; confirm indication and a recent coagulation and platelet result where relevant.
- Position supine, mild head-down to distend the vein, head turned slightly away.
- Full barrier precautions and chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation; sterile ultrasound probe cover.
- Pre-scan: confirm patency (compressible, not thrombosed) and the relationship to the carotid artery.
- Local anaesthetic, then needle entry under real-time ultrasound, visualising the needle tip entering the vein.
- Pass the guidewire; confirm its venous position on ultrasound before dilation; use pressure transduction or blood gas if uncertain. Avoid ectopy; never lose hold of the wire.
- Skin nick, dilate, advance the catheter over the wire, withdraw the wire.
- Aspirate and flush all lumens, secure, apply a sterile dressing.
- After placement, assess tip location using the appropriate ECG/imaging pathway and exclude pneumothorax where relevant. A rapid atrial swirl sign supports venous delivery but does not precisely localise the catheter tip. Account for all guidewire components.

**Complications:** arterial puncture, pneumothorax, haemothorax, air embolism, arrhythmia, cardiac tamponade (rare, from perforation), thoracic duct injury (left side), nerve injury, catheter malposition, infection, thrombosis, line fracture or embolisation.

- Safety response: if a large-bore catheter or dilator has entered an artery, leave it in place and seek urgent vascular/interventional advice; do not simply remove and compress.
- For suspected venous air embolism, stop entrainment, occlude the source, give oxygen and support circulation.
- Prevent air entry during CVC removal with appropriate positioning, respiratory timing and an occlusive dressing.

## 4.7 Ultrasound for vascular access (AT_GS 1.13)

**What ultrasound adds:** identification of the vein and its patency, anatomical variation and the position of the artery and nerve; real-time needle visualisation; verification of guidewire position; and detection of pneumothorax afterwards.

| Aspect | Details |
|---|---|
| Evidence | Systematic reviews show higher first-pass and overall success, fewer attempts and fewer complications (arterial puncture, haematoma) for the internal jugular route; benefit is clearest in the IJ and also seen for femoral and subclavian when performed by trained operators. The UK National Institute for Clinical Excellence recommended two-dimensional ultrasound guidance for elective IJ cannulation in 2002 |
| Techniques | Static (mark the site first) versus real-time dynamic; short-axis (out-of-plane) versus long-axis (in-plane) views; the short-axis view is easier to learn but can lose the needle tip |
| Other uses | Difficult peripheral cannulation; arterial line insertion; PICC insertion; regional anaesthesia; supporting venous delivery (rapid atrial swirl sign; not exact tip localisation) |
| Limitations | Operator training, equipment, sterile cover and time; poor images in obesity, oedema and some patients; does not replace anatomical knowledge or careful technique |

**Evidence:**

- Two Cochrane reviews (Brass 2015) examined real-time two-dimensional ultrasound guidance for central venous cannulation, one for the internal jugular vein and one for the subclavian and femoral veins.
- Ultrasound guidance reduces complications and failed cannulation, most clearly for the internal jugular vein; the evidence for subclavian and femoral sites is of lower certainty.

## 4.8 Presenting a vascular access procedure in a viva (AR_ME 3.2)

- Use the same eight-step structure for every access procedure: **indications; contraindications; relevant anatomy; equipment and preparation; technique; confirmation of position and use; complications and how to avoid them; aftercare and removal.** The same structure applies to peripheral and shock access (subsections 4.1 and 4.2), PICCs (subsection 4.3), central lines (subsections 4.4 to 4.7), arterial lines (topic 5) and the PAC (subsection 1.4).

**SAQ frame for "Evaluate the place of ultrasound in vascular access":** (1) rationale and mechanism; (2) evidence by site; (3) techniques; (4) other uses; (5) limitations; (6) conclusion that real-time ultrasound is the standard of care for IJ and a valuable adjunct elsewhere.

items.title: 5. Arterial blood pressure monitoring and waveform interpretation
items.body:
Direct arterial pressure monitoring gives beat-to-beat pressure, a waveform that carries information about stroke volume and vascular tone, and access for blood sampling. Its accuracy depends entirely on a correctly set up transducer system, which is why damping and natural frequency are standard exam topics.

## 5.1 Indications and contraindications

| Indications | Relative contraindications |
|---|---|
| Major surgery or anticipated rapid blood pressure change (cardiac, vascular, neurosurgical, major abdominal, thoracic) | Local infection at the insertion site |
| Significant cardiovascular or respiratory disease, shock, sepsis, ARDS | Coagulopathy or anticoagulation (more important for deep, non-compressible sites) |
| Need for frequent arterial blood gases or sampling | Inadequate collateral circulation to the limb (for example abnormal ulnar flow) |
| Controlled hypotension or hypertension | Prior vascular surgery, graft or stent at the site; arteriovenous fistula in that arm |
| Poor NIBP accuracy (morbid obesity, burns, arrhythmia, extremes of pressure) | Raynaud's disease, vasculitis, peripheral vascular disease at the site |
| Derived monitoring: pulse contour, SVV/PPV | Thoracic outlet obstruction for brachial or axillary sites |

There are no absolute contraindications. The Allen's test has poor predictive value for ischaemic complications and is not a reliable gatekeeper.

## 5.2 Sites

| Site | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| Radial | Superficial, easily accessed, collateral supply from the ulnar artery, comfortable | Distal waveform amplification (higher systolic than central), vasospasm in shock, thrombosis |
| Brachial | Larger, less spasm | Few collaterals, median nerve proximity, thrombosis risk to the forearm |
| Axillary | Large, central waveform, less affected by vasoconstriction | Brachial plexus injury, haematoma, harder to compress |
| Femoral | Large, reliable in shock, central waveform | Infection, retroperitoneal haematoma, limb ischaemia, patient mobility |
| Dorsalis pedis | Alternative when arms unavailable | Marked distal amplification, small vessel, unreliable in PVD |
| Ulnar, superficial temporal | Rare alternatives | Specialist use |

**Anatomy (radial):**

- The artery lies lateral to flexor carpi radialis tendon over the distal radius.
- The ulnar artery supplies most of the hand through the superficial palmar arch, so a functioning ulnar supply is protective.
- Distal amplification means a peripheral trace has a higher systolic and lower diastolic pressure than the aorta, while mean pressure is similar or slightly lower.

## 5.3 Technique

- Consent, equipment, sterile technique and local anaesthetic in an awake patient.
- Position (wrist extended on a roll, palm up), identify the artery by palpation or ultrasound.
- Cannulate (20 G for the radial site) by direct or catheter-through-needle or Seldinger technique; ultrasound guidance increases first-pass success.
- Connect to a flushed, bubble-free pressure tubing set with a continuous flush (about 3 mL/h) from a bag pressurised to 300 mmHg.
- Zero to atmosphere and level at the right atrium; confirm waveform and perform a fast-flush test.
- Secure the catheter, label it clearly as arterial, and check the distal limb perfusion.

## 5.4 The transducer system: natural frequency and damping

**Components:** intra-arterial cannula, short non-compliant fluid-filled tubing, three-way taps, continuous flush device, pressure bag, strain-gauge (Wheatstone bridge) transducer, amplifier and display.

**Zero and level:** zero to atmospheric pressure; level at the phlebostatic axis (heart level). A 10 cm height error is about 7.4 mmHg. For cerebral perfusion in the sitting position, level at the external auditory meatus (approximates the circle of Willis).

Dynamic response

- The arterial waveform is a complex wave made up of a fundamental frequency (the heart rate) plus harmonics.
  - The system needs a natural frequency and damping combination adequate for the clinically important harmonics.
  - A practical target is commonly >20–25 Hz with appropriate damping; higher rates demand greater bandwidth. >40 Hz may be desirable but is not a universal minimum, and 10×HR in Hz is not mathematically equivalent to 40 Hz.
- Damping coefficient (ζ) describes how quickly oscillation dies away. Optimal damping is about 0.64–0.7.
- Natural frequency increases with a shorter, wider, stiffer tube and a less dense fluid; damping increases with narrow, compliant, air-containing or kinked tubing, clots and loose connections.

| System state | Waveform | Systolic | Diastolic | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Optimal | Accurate | Accurate | Accurate | Accurate |
| Underdamped (ringing, resonance) | Spiked, overshoot | Overestimated | Underestimated | Roughly correct |
| Overdamped (bubbles, clot, kink, compliant tubing) | Flattened, slow upstroke | Underestimated | Overestimated | Roughly correct |

**Fast-flush (square wave) test:** a brisk flush produces a square pulse followed by oscillations. An optimally damped system shows one or two oscillations and quickly returns to the trace. Many oscillations indicate underdamping; no oscillation and a sluggish return indicate overdamping.

> **Examiner favourite:** MAP is usually less affected by resonance/damping than systolic or diastolic pressure, but cannot be assumed accurate in a faulty system. Check zero/level, connections, catheter patency and fast-flush response; compare with a reliable cuff or another site before treatment.

## 5.5 Interpreting the waveform

| Feature | What it reflects | Examples of abnormality |
|---|---|---|
| Upstroke slope (dP/dt) | LV contractility, outflow | Slow, anacrotic upstroke in aortic stenosis; steep in hyperdynamic states |
| Systolic peak and pulse pressure | SV and arterial compliance | Narrow in low SV, tamponade, hypovolaemia; wide in aortic regurgitation, vasodilation, stiff arteries |
| Dicrotic notch | Aortic valve closure and arterial reflections | Low or absent in vasodilatation; high in vasoconstriction; indistinct in AR |
| Diastolic runoff | SVR and diastolic compliance | Rapid fall in vasodilation or AR |
| Respiratory variation | Heart-lung interaction | Large in hypovolaemia; pulsus paradoxus in tamponade, severe asthma |
| Beat-to-beat variation | Rhythm | Pulsus alternans in severe LV failure; bisferiens pulse in AR with AS or HOCM |

## 5.6 Complications

- **Vascular:** thrombosis and occlusion (common, usually asymptomatic at the radial site), distal ischaemia (rare), haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, vasospasm.
- **Infection:** local infection and bloodstream infection, more frequent with femoral and prolonged use.
- **Haemorrhage:** accidental disconnection; also iatrogenic blood loss from frequent sampling.
- **Neural:** nerve injury (median nerve at the brachial site, brachial plexus at the axillary site).
- **Embolic and injection injury:** air or clot embolism through flushing (particularly retrograde cerebral embolism with high flush in small patients); inadvertent intra-arterial drug injection.
- **Measurement error:** damping, positioning and zeroing errors leading to incorrect treatment.

**Management and prevention:** use the lowest effective flush rate, avoid high-volume flushes, label the line, inspect the distal limb regularly, and remove the cannula promptly if ischaemia or infection is suspected.

**SAQ frame for "Discuss indications, complications and interpretation of invasive BP":** (1) indications; (2) site choice and anatomy; (3) system set-up including zeroing, natural frequency and damping; (4) waveform interpretation; (5) complications and prevention.

items.title: 6. Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy and indicators of tissue oxygenation
items.los: AT_GS 1.16; BT_PO 1.5d; SS_IC 1.29 (role of GDT component); SS_IC 1.19; BT_RT 1.27; SS_IC 1.26
items.body:
Goal-directed therapy (GDT) means using a monitor to titrate fluids, vasopressors and inotropes to predefined physiological targets in the individual patient. The modern evidence is more sceptical than the original enthusiasm: benefit has been clearest in older trials with weak control arms, and the largest contemporary trial (OPTIMISE II) was neutral.

## 6.1 Principles

- **Rationale:** major surgery and critical illness create an oxygen debt; tissue hypoperfusion (especially splanchnic) drives complications such as anastomotic leak, infection and AKI. Standard care (heart rate, blood pressure, urine output, CVP) is insensitive to flow.
- **Method:** a flow monitor (SV/CO), a valid dynamic response test, and perfusion endpoints (e.g. lactate/CRT); FTc and ScvO₂ are additional contextual variables, not interchangeable dynamic preload tests and an explicit algorithm. The protocol is the intervention, not the device.
- **Typical targets:** stroke volume optimisation (SV rises less than about 10% after a 250 mL fluid challenge), corrected flow time (about 350 ms or more with Doppler), SVV or PPV below a threshold (about 10–13%), cardiac index or DO₂I targets, and in sepsis, MAP, lactate clearance and capillary refill.
- **Timing:** early; intraoperative and the first hours after surgery. Routine escalation to supranormal oxygen-delivery targets after organ failure has not shown benefit and can cause harm; ongoing cause-directed monitoring and treatment remain essential.

### Preop

Assess cardiac/renal reserve, baseline BP, anaemia, volume losses and procedure risk. Select a monitor only if its information can alter treatment; define individual perfusion and congestion limits and plan postoperative escalation.

### Intraop

Algorithm in outline (stroke volume optimisation)

- Establish the monitor and baseline SV.
- Give a 250 mL fluid challenge over 5–10 minutes.
- If SV rises by about 10% or more, reassess perfusion and fluid tolerance. Repeat only if a further clinically useful increase is needed and there is no congestion; responsiveness alone is not an indication.
- If SV does not rise (plateau), stop fluids and treat remaining hypotension or low flow with vasopressor or, if ventricular function is poor, a low-dose inotrope.
- A fall in SV >about 10%, bleeding or changing conditions triggers reassessment of mechanism, not an automatic fluid bolus. Use a valid reversible test or a cautious measured challenge if hypovolaemia remains likely.

![Stroke volume optimisation algorithm: 5 steps, 1 decision](set10-fig3.png)

The loop repeats fluid only while perfusion remains inadequate, response is useful and fluid is tolerated. Stop when these conditions fail; identify vasodilation, pump failure or obstruction before selecting vasopressor/inotrope treatment.

### Postop

- Continue indicated pressure/flow and perfusion assessment through early recovery; review haemoglobin, pain, temperature, lactate, urine output and signs of congestion.
- Reassess the cause of hypotension, restore oral intake, stop unnecessary IV fluid and escalate evolving cardiac or organ dysfunction.
- Avoid automatic fluid/inotrope continuation after the operative indication has resolved.

## 6.2 Evidence in complex surgery (AT_GS 1.16)

| Evidence | Population | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Early trials and meta-analyses (including Cochrane) | High-risk major surgery | Fewer complications; mortality benefit mainly in studies with high baseline mortality |
| OPTIMISE (JAMA 2014) | 734 high-risk GI surgery patients | Primary composite (complications and 30-day mortality) not significantly reduced; updated meta-analysis suggested reduced complications |
| RELIEF (NEJM 2018) | Major abdominal surgery, restrictive versus liberal fluids | 3000 patients, 47 hospitals, 7 countries (ANZCA CTN and ANZICS CTG). Disability-free survival at 1 year 81.9% restrictive versus 82.3% liberal (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.88–1.24). AKI 8.6% versus 5.0%. Surgical site infection (16.5% versus 13.6%) and renal replacement therapy (0.9% versus 0.3%) were also higher with restriction but not significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Median fluid about 3.7 L versus 6.1 L |
| OPTIMISE II (BMJ 2024) | 2498 patients aged 65 or older, major elective GI surgery | Cardiac output-guided fluid with low-dose inotrope did not reduce postoperative infection (23.2% versus 22.7%) and was associated with more early cardiac events, mainly tachyarrhythmias |

OPTIMISE II (BMJ 2024;2498 patients): infections 23.2% versus 22.7%, adjusted OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.84–1.25); acute cardiac events within 24 hours 3.0% versus 1.7%, adjusted OR 1.82 (1.06–3.13), largely arrhythmias. It tested fluids plus routine low-dose inotrope, not every use of CO monitoring.

**How to answer "discuss GDT for complex surgery":**

- Present the physiological rationale and the method
- Show that early evidence suggested benefit
- Show that larger recent trials, set in modern ERAS care, are neutral
- Conclude that GDT is reasonable in selected high-risk patients (older, major abdominal or vascular, emergency laparotomy, significant comorbidity) within a protocol, with attention to the risks of inotrope-related arrhythmia and of fluid overload.

> **Examiner favourite:** distinguish GDT (individualised, physiologically targeted) from fixed restrictive or liberal fluid regimens (RELIEF) and from ERAS (a bundle of which fluid management is one part).

## 6.3 Role of GDT in shock (SS_IC 1.29 component)

| Shock type | Core treatment | Role of goal-directed monitoring |
|---|---|---|
| Septic / distributive | Antimicrobials and source control, balanced crystalloid, noradrenaline | Dynamic fluid assessment, MAP, lactate, capillary refill; echo; avoid fixed CVP/ScvO₂ targets |
| Cardiogenic | Revascularisation or treatment of cause, inotrope or vasopressor, mechanical support | PAC or echo to define LV and RV filling and output; MAP and CI targets; lactate |
| Haemorrhagic | Haemorrhage control, damage-control resuscitation with blood products, permissive hypotension in selected trauma | Lactate and base deficit for response; viscoelastic testing; limited role for fluid-based GDT |
| Obstructive | Relieve the obstruction (drain, thrombolysis, decompress) | Echo to diagnose; monitoring to follow response |

## 6.4 Goal-directed therapy in sepsis (SS_IC 1.19)

| Trial or guideline | Key point |
|---|---|
| Rivers (NEJM 2001) | Early goal-directed therapy (CVP 8–12, MAP at least 65, ScvO₂ at least 70%) reduced mortality in a single-centre study (30.5% versus 46.5%) |
| ProCESS (2014), ARISE (2014, ANZICS-led), ProMISe (2015) | Protocolised EGDT did not improve mortality compared with usual care. The pooled PRISM analysis (NEJM 2017; 3723 patients, 138 hospitals) found 90-day mortality of 24.9% with EGDT versus 25.4% with usual care (adjusted OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.82–1.14), with more ICU and cardiovascular support days and higher costs with EGDT |
| Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 | Suggests dynamic measures (passive leg raise or fluid bolus response) over static measures to guide fluid, serial lactate with capillary refill time as an adjunct, an initial MAP target of 65 mmHg (60 to 65 mmHg at age 65 or over), noradrenaline first line with vasopressin added as doses escalate, balanced crystalloids, and at least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid in the first 3 hours (weak recommendation, low-certainty evidence), individualised and reassessed |
| CLASSIC (2022), CLOVERS (2023) | Restrictive fluid strategies did not alter 90-day mortality compared with standard or liberal strategies in septic shock |

- The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 guideline (Prescott, Antonelli et al., Crit Care Med 2026) suggests at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours (low certainty), individualised and reassessed
- Prefers balanced crystalloids to saline (saline in traumatic brain injury)
- Recommends against starches and suggests against gelatin
- Favours dynamic measures (passive leg raise or fluid bolus response) over physical examination or static measures
- Sets an initial MAP target of 65 mmHg (60–65 mmHg at age 65 or over)
- Uses noradrenaline first line, adding vasopressin as doses escalate and adrenaline if MAP remains inadequate
- Starts vasopressors peripherally rather than delaying
- And suggests serial lactate to guide resuscitation, with capillary refill time as an adjunct.

**Key messages:**

- Early recognition and treatment matter more than any single haemodynamic target
- Fixed protocol targets (CVP, ScvO₂) are not required
- Resuscitate to perfusion indicators (MAP, lactate, capillary refill, urine output) and re-assess
- Fluid is given in boluses with reassessment of response
- Norepinephrine early and vasopressin or hydrocortisone added in escalating shock.

- Current monitoring nuance: ESICM 2025 favours echo first, dynamic response testing, and CO/SV monitoring in shock unresponsive to initial treatment.
- SSC 2026 finds insufficient outcome evidence to recommend routine minimally/non-invasive CO devices for all septic-shock patients.
- These positions support selective, question-driven monitoring rather than a device for every patient.

**SAQ frame for "Discuss the role of goal-directed therapy":** (1) definition and rationale; (2) monitors and targets; (3) algorithm; (4) evidence for and against; (5) patients likely to benefit; (6) risks; (7) application in shock and sepsis.

Blood pressure describes pressure, while cardiac output measures global flow; lactate, base deficit and venous oxygen saturation tell you whether flow is adequate for metabolic demand. No single indicator is reliable on its own, so resuscitation is guided by trends in a combination of them, checked against the clinical picture.

## 6.5 The physiological question

Tissues are adequately oxygenated when delivery (DO₂) meets consumption (VO₂) at a sufficient extraction ratio. When DO₂ falls below a critical value, extraction can no longer compensate, VO₂ becomes supply-dependent, ATP production shifts towards anaerobic glycolysis, and lactate and base deficit rise while mixed venous saturation falls.

Indicators are either **global** (lactate, base deficit, SvO₂/ScvO₂, venous-arterial CO₂ gap) or **regional/peripheral** (capillary refill time, skin mottling, urine output, near-infrared spectroscopy of tissue, sublingual microcirculation). Global indicators can look normal while a regional bed is ischaemic (for example the gut).

## 6.6 Lactate

- **Source and clearance:** produced by glycolysis; cleared mainly by the liver (and kidney); normal below about 2 mmol/L.

A falling lactate is a useful response marker, but “lactate clearance” is a change in concentration, not a direct clearance measurement. If peripheral perfusion and haemodynamics have recovered, investigate ongoing adrenergic production, impaired metabolism or regional ischaemia rather than giving fluid until lactate is normal.

- Type A (oxygen supply–demand imbalance): hypoperfusion, severe hypoxaemia or anaemia. Seizures and intense muscle work may raise lactate through high glycolytic flux without systemic shock.
- **Type B (non-hypoxic):** adrenaline and β₂ stimulation (accelerated aerobic glycolysis in sepsis), liver failure, metformin, thiamine deficiency, malignancy, propofol infusion syndrome, salbutamol and other drugs.
- **Use:** a raised initial lactate (above 2 mmol/L, and especially above 4 mmol/L) is a marker of severity and mortality in sepsis, trauma and after cardiac surgery.
  - Serial lactate and lactate clearance are more informative than a single value, and guiding resuscitation to a falling lactate is endorsed in sepsis guidance.
  - A trial of lactate clearance (at least 10% in the first hours) was non-inferior to ScvO₂ targets (Jones, JAMA 2010).
- **Limitations:** liver dysfunction (poor clearance), type B causes, arterial versus venous sampling (use consistent sampling; agreement worsens at high concentrations), delayed fall even after restored perfusion.
  - Hartmann’s contains sodium lactate, not lactic acid.
  - It may transiently raise measured lactate, especially with rapid large volumes or impaired metabolism; prevent sampling contamination from the infusion line and interpret the trend clinically.

## 6.7 Base deficit

- Arterial base deficit (negative base excess) reflects metabolic acidosis from any cause.
- In trauma, it estimates the degree of shock and predicts transfusion need and mortality; a commonly used grading is mild (3–5 mmol/L), moderate (6–9) and severe (10 or more) (Davis).
- **Limitations:** hyperchloraemic acidosis from large saline volumes, ethanol and ketones, renal failure, and chronic respiratory compensation. It correlates with lactate but is not specific for hypoperfusion; interpret together.

## 6.8 Mixed venous (SvO₂) and central venous (ScvO₂) oxygen saturation

SvO₂ fraction ≈ SaO₂ fraction − VO₂/[CO × Hb × 1.34 × 10], with VO₂ in mL/min, CO in L/min and Hb in g/dL; use ×100 for saturation in percent

|  | SvO₂ | ScvO₂ |
|---|---|---|
| Sample site | Pulmonary artery (true mixed venous blood) | SVC sample, mainly upper-body venous blood; RA samples have variable admixture |
| Normal | about 65–75% | often slightly lower than SvO₂ in health; no fixed offset |
| In shock | Reflects whole body | Often higher than SvO₂ in shock, but the difference is variable and the values are not interchangeable |
| Access | PAC | Central line |

**Interpreting a low value:** DO₂ is low relative to VO₂ (low cardiac output, anaemia, hypoxaemia) or VO₂ is high (fever, shivering, pain, thyrotoxicosis). Treat the cause: flow, haemoglobin, oxygen or demand.

**Interpreting a normal or high value:** does not exclude hypoperfusion. In sepsis, impaired oxygen extraction (microcirculatory shunting, mitochondrial dysfunction) causes a high SvO₂/ScvO₂ despite tissue hypoxia; also seen in cyanide poisoning, hypothermia and left-to-right shunts. A wedged PAC sample reads falsely high.

**Evidence:** Rivers' EGDT set an ScvO₂ target of at least 70%; ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe did not show a benefit of protocolised ScvO₂ monitoring over usual care, so it is no longer a mandatory target. In high-risk surgery, a low perioperative ScvO₂ is associated with complications and may prompt investigation of flow and haemoglobin.

## 6.9 Other indicators

ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025) extends the 2019 trial: a personalised CRT-guided protocol improved a hierarchical composite, mainly through shorter vital support. Keep this distinct from a mortality benefit, and use CRT with pressure, flow, responsiveness and clinical assessment.

| Indicator | Principle | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Venous-arterial CO₂ gap (Pv-aCO₂) | Rises when flow is low relative to CO₂ production (greater than about 6 mmHg is abnormal) | Complements ScvO₂ when saturation is high |
| Capillary refill time and skin mottling | Peripheral perfusion | Rapid, no equipment; used as a resuscitation target in ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019), where a CRT-targeted strategy showed a trend to lower mortality versus lactate-targeted (not statistically significant) |
| Near-infrared spectroscopy (StO₂) | Tissue haemoglobin oxygenation in muscle, brain | Limited by oedema, skin colour, variable validation |
| Urine output | Renal perfusion | Slow and non-specific |
| Gastric tonometry, sublingual microscopy | Splanchnic and microcirculation | Mostly research |

## 6.10 Using the indicators in resuscitation

| Indicator | What it tells you | Main strength | Main weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lactate | Global anaerobic metabolism or stress | Prognostic; trend guides therapy | Slow; type B causes; liver clearance |
| Base deficit | Metabolic acidosis | Trauma severity | Non-specific; confounded by saline and ethanol |
| SvO₂ / ScvO₂ | Balance of DO₂ and VO₂ | Detects inadequate flow | Normal or high in sepsis despite hypoperfusion |
| Pv-aCO₂ gap | Adequacy of flow | Useful when ScvO₂ is normal | Needs central venous and arterial samples |
| Capillary refill | Peripheral perfusion | Rapid and cheap | Subjective; affected by temperature |

> **Examiner favourite:** do not chase a single number. Use lactate and base deficit as global severity markers, ScvO₂ and the CO₂ gap to understand flow, and capillary refill and urine output to confirm clinical response; correct the cause rather than the number.

> **Viva line:** "A normal blood pressure does not mean adequate perfusion. I would look for evidence of hypoperfusion with lactate, base deficit and capillary refill, and track the response over time, not a single reading."

> **SAQ frame:** (1) physiology of delivery and extraction; (2) each indicator with how it works, interpretation, and limitations; (3) how to combine them; (4) pitfalls (sepsis, liver failure, saline acidosis).

items.title: 7. Perioperative fluid requirements and intravenous fluid choice
items.body:
For a low-risk patient having low-risk surgery, the prescription is simple: allow clear fluids until two hours before surgery, give a balanced crystalloid at a modest maintenance rate, replace measured losses, treat vasodilation with a vasopressor before pouring in fluid, and reassess. For higher-risk patients move to individualised, monitor-guided therapy (topic 6).

## 7.1 Factors determining perioperative fluid requirements

| Factor | Considerations |
|---|---|
| Pre-existing deficit | Fasting (minimal if clear fluids are allowed until 2 hours before surgery), bowel preparation, vomiting, diarrhoea, bleeding, sepsis, diuretics, poor intake |
| Maintenance | Water, sodium and potassium requirements: roughly 25–30 mL/kg/day water, 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium and potassium |
| Intra-operative losses | Blood loss, evaporative loss from open body cavities, interstitial redistribution (the older concept of a fixed "third space" loss is not supported) |
| Anaesthetic effects | Vasodilation and venodilation from anaesthetic drugs and neuraxial block (relative hypovolaemia) |
| Patient | Age, cardiac, renal and hepatic disease, diabetes, electrolyte disorders, pregnancy, sepsis, weight |
| Surgery | Duration, type, expected blood loss, bowel handling, laparoscopic versus open, ERAS pathway |
| Monitoring and response | Clinical signs, urine output (a poor guide), lactate, dynamic indices |

**Revised Starling principle:**

- Fluid moves across the capillary wall according to the glycocalyx-endothelial model, not simply according to hydrostatic and oncotic gradients on either side of the vessel wall.
- In health, the intravascular fraction of crystalloid changes with infusion rate, time, vascular tone, anaesthesia, hydration and capillary integrity; no fixed 20–25% retention rule applies.
- Inflammation can increase interstitial accumulation.
- Colloids are not retained as efficiently in inflamed states as older teaching suggested.

## 7.2 Calculating requirements: low-risk patient, low-risk surgery (IT_GS 1.6)

### Preop

Review oral intake and fasting, gastrointestinal/renal losses, bleeding, electrolytes and fluid-sensitive disease. Permit clear fluids within the locally approved fasting pathway; two hours is conventional, while approved liberal protocols may differ. Correct a demonstrated deficit and plan blood/access requirements.

### Intraop

Historical calculation (4-2-1 rule)

| Weight band | Rate |
|---|---|
| First 10 kg | 4 mL/kg/h |
| Next 10 kg | 2 mL/kg/h |
| Each kg above 20 kg | 1 mL/kg/h |

The historical 4-2-1 calculation gives 110 mL/h for 70 kg; this is not an obligatory adult requirement (it equals about 38 mL/kg/day). Routine adult maintenance is usually 25–30 mL/kg/day, reduced in frailty or cardiac/renal impairment. Intraop rates depend on the operation, oral intake and losses; an illustrative low-risk starting rate of 1–2 mL/kg/h requires reassessment.

**Deficit:** if the patient fasted from food but drank clear fluids until two hours before surgery, no routine deficit replacement is needed. With prolonged fasting or gastrointestinal loss, assess actual volume/electrolyte deficit and replace it in reassessed increments. Do not calculate an automatic replacement bolus as fasting hours × 4-2-1 rate.

- Losses: estimate blood loss and the physiological response, then use measured crystalloid aliquots or blood components as appropriate.
- A fixed crystalloid 3:1/colloid 1:1 replacement ratio is unreliable and risks overload; major haemorrhage requires the local blood-product protocol.
- The historical 2/4/6–8 mL/kg/h “exposure/third-space” allowances are not validated contemporary replacement targets.
- Replace demonstrable losses and reassess flow, perfusion, haemoglobin and congestion.

**Worked example:**

- 70 kg adult, laparoscopic cholecystectomy lasting 90 minutes, clear fluids until two hours pre-op.
- An illustrative 1–2 mL/kg/h gives 105–210 mL over 90 minutes; no deficit; negligible blood loss; evaporative loss small.
- A total of 500–1000 mL might be reasonable for some patients, but is not a required minimum or maximum; titrate to baseline status, actual losses, duration and response.
- Treat predominantly anaesthetic vasodilation with an appropriate vasopressor rather than obligatory fluid loading.
- Liberal volumes of crystalloid (up to 20–30 mL/kg) have been used to reduce nausea and dizziness in minor ambulatory surgery, but the benefit is modest and must be weighed against fluid overload.

### Postop

Resume oral/enteral intake early when safe. Stop IV fluid when no longer needed; otherwise prescribe maintenance separately from replacement and resuscitation, including glucose/electrolyte needs. Review weight, balance, renal function, sodium, potassium and congestion; do not treat isolated oliguria with repeated blind boluses.

## 7.3 Choice of fluid

| Fluid | Composition (approximate) | Comments |
|---|---|---|
| 0.9% sodium chloride | Na⁺ 154, Cl⁻ 154 mmol/L; pH about 5.5; osmolality 308 | Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with large volumes; often selected in TBI to avoid hypotonic fluids; hyponatraemia treatment depends on mechanism and symptoms (isotonic saline may worsen SIADH, while severe symptoms require hypertonic saline) |
| Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann's) | Na⁺ 131, K⁺ 5, Ca²⁺ 2, Cl⁻ 111, lactate 29 mmol/L; osmolality about 278 | Balanced; slightly hypotonic (avoid in raised ICP); contains calcium (do not mix with citrated blood in the same line) |
| Plasma-Lyte 148 | Na⁺ 140, K⁺ 5, Mg²⁺ 1.5, Cl⁻ 98, acetate 27, gluconate 23 mmol/L; osmolality about 294 | Balanced, near-isotonic; no calcium |
| 5% dextrose | Glucose 50 g/L | Provides free water once glucose is metabolised; not a resuscitation fluid |
| Albumin 4–5% | Colloid; oncotic pressure | SAFE study (ANZICS): no difference from saline overall; harm in TBI follow-up; a sepsis subgroup signal does not establish routine benefit |
| Hydroxyethyl starch | Synthetic colloid | Avoid in sepsis/critical illness: 6S found increased mortality and RRT; CHEST found more RRT without a significant mortality difference |
| Gelatin | Synthetic colloid | Anaphylaxis risk and uncertain benefit; SSC 2026 suggests against use in sepsis |

**Evidence for balanced crystalloids:** SPLIT (JAMA 2015, New Zealand), SMART (NEJM 2018), SALT-ED, PLUS (NEJM 2022, ANZICS) and BaSICS found small or no differences between balanced solutions and saline in mortality; SMART showed a small reduction in major adverse kidney events with balanced crystalloids. Balanced crystalloids are the default for most perioperative use.

> **Examiner favourite:** choose the fluid for the problem. Replace blood loss with blood; replace extracellular volume with a balanced isotonic crystalloid; avoid hypotonic dextrose-containing fluids in children and in patients at risk of hyponatraemia, except where specifically indicated.

> **SAQ frame:** (1) components of requirement (maintenance, deficit, losses); (2) calculation for a typical case; (3) choice of fluid by composition and evidence; (4) risks of too little and too much fluid; (5) when to move to monitor-guided therapy.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
Examiners expect you to name the trial, say what it tested, give the headline result and say why it changed practice. This table pulls together every trial cited in this set.

## 8.1 Cardiac output monitoring and filling pressures

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marik et al., Chest 2008 | Systematic review: CVP versus blood volume and fluid response | Pooled correlation of CVP with blood volume 0.16; CVP did not predict response to a fluid challenge | Foundation of the "CVP cannot guide fluids" argument |
| Marik and Cavallazzi, Crit Care Med 2013 | Updated meta-analysis (43 studies) | AUC 0.56 (95% CI 0.54–0.58); correlation 0.18; same in ICU and operating room; 57% responders | CVP is not a basis for fluid decisions |
| Marik et al., Crit Care Med 2009 | Systematic review of dynamic arterial waveform indices | AUC 0.94 PPV, 0.84 SVV, 0.86 SPV versus 0.55 CVP; valid only with controlled ventilation | Why dynamic indices replaced static pressures |
| SUPPORT (Connors, JAMA 1996) | Observational cohort, 5735 ICU patients | PAC associated with higher 30-day mortality (OR about 1.24) | Triggered the PAC trials; association, not proof of harm |
| Sandham, NEJM 2003 | RCT of PAC-guided GDT in elderly high-risk surgical patients | No mortality benefit; more pulmonary emboli in the PAC group | PAC not routinely useful in high-risk surgery |
| PAC-Man (Harvey, Lancet 2005) | Pragmatic RCT, 65 UK ICUs, over 1000 patients | Hospital mortality 68% versus 66%; adjusted HR 1.09 (0.94–1.27) | No clear benefit or harm; PAC not an intervention itself |
| ESCAPE (JAMA 2005) | RCT in advanced heart failure | No difference in days alive and out of hospital | No primary benefit; more in-hospital adverse events with PAC (21.9% vs 11.5%) |
| FACTT (NEJM 2006) | RCT in acute lung injury: PAC versus CVC, and fluid strategy | No benefit of PAC; conservative fluid strategy improved ventilator-free days | Fluid strategy mattered more than the monitor |
| Rajaram, Cochrane 2013 | Meta-analysis of 13 trials, 5686 patients | No difference in mortality, ICU stay or cost | Confirms neutrality of PAC in ICU and high-risk surgery |

## 8.2 Goal-directed therapy and perioperative fluids

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| OPTIMISE (Pearse, JAMA 2014) | RCT, 734 patients, major GI surgery, cardiac output-guided algorithm | Primary composite not significantly reduced; meta-analysis suggested fewer complications | Equivocal evidence for flow-guided therapy |
| OPTIMISE II (BMJ 2024) | RCT, 2498 patients aged 65 or older, major elective GI surgery | Postoperative infection 23.2% versus 22.7%; more early cardiac events with the intervention | Contemporary trial: cardiac output-guided fluid and low-dose inotrope did not help |
| RELIEF (Myles, NEJM 2018) | RCT, 3000 patients, major abdominal surgery, restrictive versus liberal fluids | Disability-free survival at 1 year 81.9% versus 82.3% (HR 1.05); AKI 8.6% versus 5.0% | Restriction is not better and increases AKI; ANZCA and ANZICS-led trial |
| SAFE (NEJM 2004) | RCT, ICU, albumin versus saline | No overall difference; harm in traumatic brain injury subgroup | No overall mortality advantage in SAFE’s population; avoid in TBI and individualise other indications |
| SPLIT (JAMA 2015), SMART (NEJM 2018), PLUS (NEJM 2022) | Balanced crystalloid versus saline in critically ill patients | Little or no difference in mortality; SMART showed fewer major adverse kidney events | Balanced crystalloids are a reasonable default |
| 6S and CHEST | Hydroxyethyl starch versus crystalloid in ICU | More renal replacement therapy with starch | Starches should not be used in the critically ill |

## 8.3 Shock, sepsis and perfusion targets

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rivers, NEJM 2001 | Single-centre RCT of early goal-directed therapy (CVP, MAP, ScvO₂ targets) | Large mortality reduction (30.5% versus 46.5%) | Launched EGDT; not reproduced |
| ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe | Three multicentre RCTs of EGDT versus usual care (ARISE was Australasian) | No mortality benefit in any trial | Protocolised EGDT abandoned |
| PRISM (NEJM 2017) | Individual patient data meta-analysis of the three trials, 3723 patients | 90-day mortality 24.9% versus 25.4%; adjusted OR 0.97 (0.82–1.14); higher costs with EGDT | No benefit overall or in the examined prespecified subgroups; absence of a detected interaction does not prove no individual can benefit |
| CLASSIC (2022), CLOVERS (2023) | RCTs of restrictive versus standard or liberal fluids in septic shock | No difference in 90-day mortality | Neither tested strategy was superior after initial fluids; this does not make fluid dose irrelevant or establish equivalence in every shock phenotype |
| ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (JAMA 2019) | RCT: capillary refill-targeted versus lactate-targeted resuscitation | Trend to lower mortality with capillary refill targeting, not statistically significant | Peripheral perfusion is a legitimate target |
| ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (JAMA 2025) | Early septic shock; 1501 randomised, 1467 in primary analysis; personalised CRT protocol vs usual care | Hierarchical 28-day composite win ratio 1.16 (95% CI 1.02–1.33; P=.04), driven mainly by shorter vital support | Supports a personalised CRT-based protocol; does not prove a stand-alone mortality reduction or that CRT alone is sufficient |

## 8.4 Vascular access

| Trial | Design | Headline result | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chopra, Lancet 2013 | Meta-analysis of PICC and venous thromboembolism | PICCs carried a higher risk of DVT than other central lines in hospitalised patients (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.54 to 4.23, in 11 comparative studies; number needed to harm about 26) | PICC is not automatically the safer central line |
| Brass, Cochrane 2015 | Meta-analysis of ultrasound for central venous cannulation | Ultrasound guidance reduces failure and complications, most clearly for the IJ | Basis for ultrasound as standard of care |

**Exam technique for trials:** give the name and year, the population, the intervention and comparator, the primary outcome and result, and one sentence on the implication or limitation (for example single-centre, usual care changed, surrogate endpoint). Do not quote figures you are not sure of; a correct qualitative statement scores better than a confident wrong number.

## Evidence, examiner verification and coverage map (Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content)

Clinical/content review: **3 November 2026**. Historical questions are answered using current guidance. These model answers and self-marking checklists are teaching syntheses, not official marking schemes; priority labels are retained from the supplied bank, not fresh validated exam predictions. Recent publication supports study relevance, not a prediction of what examiners will ask.

### Examiner-report verification

Directly checked supplied reports: 2026.1 Q2 (PDF p13), 2025.2 Q8 (p20), 2025.1 Q1 (p15), 2023.2 Q4 (p11), and 2015.2 Q9 (pp7–8). Added 2015.2 Q7 (p7), including its reported 50.3% pass rate. The reports support the quoted examiner emphasis; the fuller clinical answers also use the sources below.

The original reports for **2017.1 Q7, 2013.2 Q3, 2013.1 Q3 and 2007.1 Q5** were not available among the supplied project files for this audit. Their supplied stem/pass-rate metadata are retained without claiming direct report verification. Secondary web listings do not substitute for an original report. Relevant 2023.2 and 2025.1 MCQ lists support the relevance of PAC haemorrhage and vasopressor extravasation but are not SAQ marking rubrics.

### Coverage map

| Learn domain | Existing practice retained and corrected | Added practice |
|---|---|---|
| CO/CVP/PAC, responsiveness and interpretation | CVP, PAC evaluation/insertion, CO devices, dynamic tests and SvO2 | Integrated numerical PAC/Fick/DO2 case, venous-return/CVP waves/wedge checks, PAC haemorrhage |
| Echo and POCUS | Unstable intraoperative TTE, focused assessment, Doppler, TOE and undifferentiated shock | Congestion/tolerance case; source-focused scanning, B-lines/VExUS, pneumothorax signs, documentation and limits of one TOE view |
| Monitoring standards and equipment | Previously under-represented | Remote-location monitoring SAQ-style question; PG18, PS55, handover, axillary-dissection prompts |
| Vascular access and infusion | Rapid infusion, PICC/CVC, IO, difficult PIV and arterial injury | Verified past intra-arterial-injection SAQ; peripheral-noradrenaline/extravasation question and short prompts |
| Arterial BP monitoring | Obesity, damping, sites and complications | Safer troubleshooting language and updated complication prevention |
| GDT and oxygenation/perfusion | GDT, lactate, SvO2, CRT and sepsis | Corrected contemporary trial interpretation including ARISE FLUIDS, units, need/response/tolerance and a fluid de-escalation case |
| Adult fluids | Major-surgery requirements/fluid choice | Low-risk 70 kg/90-minute fluid prescription with Preop/Intraop/Postop structure |

### Current guidelines and standards

- [ANZCA PG18, anaesthesia monitoring 2025](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/6296ef66-b43b-4dc6-938b-770f94ba7e6e/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG18%28A%29-Guideline-on-monitoring-during-anaesthesia-2017.PDF): read the current document date despite the legacy filename; includes the axillary-dissection appendix. Exact modality-specific requirements take precedence over a short model answer.
- [ANZCA PS55, minimum facilities, including Appendix 2 updated 2026](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/9b0c33f8-6a0f-4f76-9e90-a751dc181f12/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PS55-Minimum-safe-facilities-2021-%28Apdx-2-2026%29.pdf?language=en): facilities/equipment, staffing, emergency drugs and safe anaesthetising locations.
- [ANZCA PG46 2025](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/59f8ec2b-8327-4df2-9db3-b247fbb0d649/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG46%28POM%29-Cardiac-ultrasound-2014.pdf?language=en) and [PG47 2025](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/8ca3291d-4f5b-4434-8433-78bfcd239b7f/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG47-Perioperative-diagnostic-POCUS-2025.pdf?language=en): training/scope for comprehensive echo/basic TOE versus focused POCUS. A course alone is not equivalent to independent competence.
- [ESICM circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring guideline 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41236566/): clinical assessment, echo, dynamic response testing and selection of monitoring.
- [SSC 2026 official recommendations](https://www.sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/surviving-sepsis-campaign-international-guidelines-for-management-of-sepsis-and-septic-shock-2026): initial and subsequent fluids, vasopressors and integrated perfusion reassessment; distinguish conditional advice from fixed targets for every patient.
- [Association of Anaesthetists safe vascular access 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12519924/): selection, ultrasound, guidewire/arterial safety, vein preservation, peripheral vasopressors and device care. Catheter diameter/area and device-specific ratio recommendations are not interchangeable.
- [ASE right-heart guideline 2025](https://www.asecho.org/guideline/right-heart-in-adults-pulmonary-hypertension/) and [diastolic-function guideline 2025](https://www.asecho.org/guideline/left-ventricular-diastolic-function-by-echo/): multiparameter interpretation, not one TAPSE/IVC/E/e′ value in isolation.
- [NICE CG174 adult IV fluids](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg174/chapter/Recommendations) and [NG180 perioperative care](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng180/chapter/Recommendations): maintenance/replacement/resuscitation and perioperative fluid decisions.
- [ACSQHC peripheral-IV clinical care standard 2021](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/standards/clinical-care-standards/management-peripheral-intravenous-catheters-clinical-care-standard): appropriate access, asepsis, assessment, escalation and removal.

### BJA Education and Blue Book reading

- [Gilbert-Kawai, Chen and Patel. Pulmonary artery catheterisation. BJA Education 2024;24:447–457](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11589280/), with its [2025 corrigendum](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40041446/): waveforms, physiology, wedge validity, derived calculations and complications. Check equation units rather than copying formula typography.
- [Desai and Garry. Assessing dynamic fluid-responsiveness using transthoracic echocardiography. BJA Education 2018;18:218–226](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807830/): PLR/VTI, challenges and validity conditions; interpret historical thresholds alongside current guidance.
- [Walsh et al. Prevention and management of complications associated with arterial catheters. BJA Education 2025;25:173–180](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12009087/): arterial anatomy, insertion, waveform/maintenance hazards and prevention.
- [Broader applications of arterial pressure waveform analysis. CEACCP 2014;14:285–290](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-pdf/14/6/285/686578/mkt078.pdf): foundational pressure/flow concepts; contemporary device algorithms and outcome evidence differ.
- [McMullan and Silversides. Fluids in sepsis. BJA Education 2026;26:334–343](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42453803/): Full text directly reviewed through the ANZCA ClinicalKey session: glycocalyx physiology, fluid stewardship and de-escalation. Trial interpretation was cross-checked against primary reports; responsiveness does not imply tolerance.
- [Flower et al. Point-of-care ultrasound in shock. BJA Education 2026;26:464–472](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42924199/): Full text directly reviewed through the ANZCA ClinicalKey session: integrated cardiac/lung/abdominal scanning, serial assessment, diagnostic limits and governance.
- [Blue Book 2025](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1305): Kim/Lau, B-lines and beyond (pp3–20), supports lung findings and their limits. Schuller/Ly, Counting the waves (pp21–42), and Ruberry, Pulse oximetry (pp43–58), are supporting monitoring reading, not a reason to move all neuro/respiratory device physics into Set 10. Arduini et al., Sip Til Send (pp183–196), informs locally governed fasting pathways.
- [Blue Book archive](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29): Dennis, Goal-directed transthoracic echocardiography (2015), and Bath/Deacon/Jones, Preventing vascular damage during central venous catheter insertion via the internal jugular vein (2019), are foundational reading. Historical complication percentages and older PS46 terminology should not be used as current universal standards.

- [ESICM fluid-removal guideline 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40828463/): de-escalation after acute resuscitation, diuretic-based removal and limits on routine extracorporeal removal; recommendations also discussed in the directly reviewed sepsis article.

### Primary reports for important results

- [OPTIMISE 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24842135/) and [OPTIMISE II 2024](https://www.bmj.com/content/387/bmj-2024-080439): distinguish the exact intervention, primary outcome and harm signal from a claim about all GDT.
- [RELIEF 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29742967/): restrictive regimen did not improve disability-free survival and increased AKI; it does not define one optimal volume for every operation.
- [ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2019](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30772908/) and [ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41159835/): distinguish nonsignificant superiority mortality results from a later positive hierarchical composite; neither is a non-inferiority result proving CRT alone replaces other assessment.
- [SMART](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29485925/), [PLUS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35041780/), [6S](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22738085/) and [CHEST](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23075127/): endpoints and populations differ; avoid merging their findings into one claim.
- [Sandham](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12510037/), [PAC-Man](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16084255/), [ESCAPE](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/745314) and [FACTT](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa061895): selected PAC use may answer important questions despite no routine outcome benefit in the tested populations.
- [CLASSIC 2022](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2202707) and [CLOVERS 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10685906/): no significant primary mortality benefit from restrictive strategies after initial fluid; neither tested withholding all initial fluid.
- [ARISE FLUIDS 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42274006/): primary abstract verified; earlier vasopressors/lower fluid did not improve days alive and out of hospital at day 90; lower pulmonary oedema was a safety finding.
- [CVP meta-analysis 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23774337/): poor prediction of fluid responsiveness; trending CVP alone does not solve the limitation.

### Access and scope

The supplied Learn document was used to map coverage, not as independent proof of every claim. Public guidelines, accessible articles/Blue Book material and primary-trial reports were used where available. **Miller's, Yao and Kaplan were not directly checked through an authenticated textbook session.** Links identify the intended source; some publishers require institutional sign-in, and automated access failures do not establish that an article was read in full. The two 2026 BJAEd reviews above were subsequently read in full; four older examiner reports remain unverified. This targeted update does not establish that every BJAEd issue or textbook chapter has been checked. Cross-set concepts are supporting practice; aortic-dissection management remains in Set 14.

items.title: State the Fick principle and how it is used to measure cardiac output.
items.q: State the Fick principle and how it is used to measure cardiac output.
items.a:
- Cardiac output = oxygen consumption / (arterial minus venous oxygen content).
- Needs a mixed venous sample from the pulmonary artery.
- Direct Fick is the reference method but is rarely practical; assumed VO2 gives an indirect Fick estimate with additional error.
- Partial CO2 rebreathing is a separate Fick-based technique; indirect oxygen-Fick means using estimated rather than measured VO2.


> **Closing point:** Flow equals uptake divided by the arteriovenous difference.

items.title: How does pulmonary artery thermodilution work and what are its errors?
items.q: How does pulmonary artery thermodilution work and what are its errors?
items.a:
- Cold bolus injected in the RA; temperature change measured at the PA thermistor.
- Area under the curve is inversely proportional to flow (Stewart-Hamilton).
- Low output gives a large, slow curve; high output a small, fast curve.
- Errors: tricuspid regurgitation, intracardiac shunt, irregular injection, respiratory cycle timing, rapid IV fluid.


> **Closing point:** Average three injections that agree within 10%.

items.title: Compare transpulmonary thermodilution and PAC thermodilution.
items.q: Compare transpulmonary thermodilution and PAC thermodilution.
items.a:
- Injection via CVC, detection by a femoral or axillary arterial thermistor (PiCCO, EV1000).
- Gives CO, global end-diastolic volume, extravascular lung water and SVV.
- Needs calibration; less invasive than a PAC.
- Errors: shunt, aortic aneurysm, regurgitant valves, ECMO.


> **Closing point:** Calibrated systems drift less than uncalibrated ones.

items.title: How does pulse contour analysis estimate cardiac output and when is it unreliable?
items.q: How does pulse contour analysis estimate cardiac output and when is it unreliable?
items.a:
- Stroke volume derived from arterial waveform area and arterial compliance.
- Calibrated (PiCCO, LiDCO) or uncalibrated (FloTrac, Vigileo).
- Unreliable with: damping, arrhythmias, aortic regurgitation, IABP, rapid change in vascular tone.
- Track the trend rather than the absolute value.


> **Closing point:** Changes in vascular tone invalidate the compliance estimate.

items.title: How does oesophageal Doppler measure flow and what are its limits?
items.q: How does oesophageal Doppler measure flow and what are its limits?
items.a:
- Probe in the distal oesophagus measures velocity in the descending aorta.
- Flow time corrected (FTc) and peak velocity are influenced by filling, afterload, rate and contractility; neither is a pure measure of one property.
- Assumes about 70% of cardiac output goes to the descending aorta.
- Limits: operator dependence, probe position, awake patient intolerance, oesophageal pathology.


> **Closing point:** Position the probe for the best aortic signal.

items.title: How does bioreactance or bioimpedance measure cardiac output?
items.q: How does bioreactance or bioimpedance measure cardiac output?
items.a:
- Electrodes on the chest measure thoracic impedance (or phase shift).
- Changes with each stroke relate to aortic blood volume.
- Fully non-invasive.
- Limits: diathermy, arrhythmia, lung water, movement, obesity.


> **Closing point:** Convenience does not establish accuracy or reliable trending in an unstable patient.

items.title: What is a percentage error of 30% and why does it matter?
items.q: What is a percentage error of 30% and why does it matter?
items.a:
- Critchley and Critchley criterion for a new CO monitor against a reference method.
- The historical 30% criterion assumed particular reference/test precision; neither 20% nor 30% is a universal property.
- Many minimally invasive monitors fail in extremes of vascular tone.
- Trending ability needs a separate polar plot analysis.


> **Closing point:** Agreement of trend can be better than agreement of absolute value.

items.title: Which PAC measurements are directly measured and which are derived?
items.q: Which PAC measurements are directly measured and which are derived?
items.a:
- Measured: RA, PA and wedge pressures, thermodilution CO, SvO2, temperature.
- Derived: SVR, PVR, stroke volume, indexed variables.
- SVR = (MAP − CVP) × 80 / CO.
- PVR = (mPAP − PAOP) × 80 / CO.


> **Closing point:** Derived values multiply the error in the measured ones.

items.title: Why does CVP fail as a guide to volume status?
items.q: Why does CVP fail as a guide to volume status?
items.a:
- Reflects RA pressure, not volume.
- Confounded by compliance, intrathoracic pressure, PEEP, valve disease, RV function and tricuspid disease.
- Zero level and transducer position change the value.
- Weak relationship to fluid responsiveness (area under the curve about 0.56 in meta-analysis).


> **Closing point:** A CVP number cannot predict a response; even a CVP change alone cannot establish a flow response.

items.title: Describe the physiology of pulse pressure and stroke volume variation.
items.q: Describe the physiology of pulse pressure and stroke volume variation.
items.a:
- Positive pressure inspiration reduces RV preload and can transiently increase LV filling by pulmonary blood displacement and reduce LV afterload; RV afterload may rise.
- The fall in venous return shows in LV stroke volume a few beats later.
- A preload-dependent ventricle shows greater variation.
- Thresholds: PPV above 13% and SVV above 10 to 12% predict a response.


> **Closing point:** Heart-lung interaction acts as a built-in fluid challenge.

items.title: List the conditions needed for PPV and SVV to be valid.
items.q: List the conditions needed for PPV and SVV to be valid.
items.a:
- Controlled ventilation without spontaneous effort.
- Classical validation used around 8 mL/kg predicted body weight; a brief supervised tidal-volume challenge may help. Do not abandon lung-protective ventilation merely to use PPV.
- Sinus rhythm.
- Closed chest, normal intra-abdominal pressure.
- Normal RV function and compliance.


> **Closing point:** Choose another test whenever validity conditions fail.

items.title: How do you perform a passive leg raise and interpret it?
items.q: How do you perform a passive leg raise and interpret it?
items.a:
- Semi-recumbent to supine with legs raised 45 degrees for 1 minute.
- Moves about 300 mL from the legs and abdomen.
- A rise in stroke volume or cardiac output of 10% or more predicts a response.
- Valid in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia; measure flow, not blood pressure.


> **Closing point:** It is a reversible fluid challenge.

items.title: What is the end-expiratory occlusion test?
items.q: What is the end-expiratory occlusion test?
items.a:
- Hold expiration for 15 seconds in a ventilated patient.
- Venous return rises without inspiratory impedance.
- A small CO/SV rise around 5% may predict response if the monitor is sufficiently precise; pressure alone is not an equivalent flow endpoint.
- Needs an uninterrupted hold and a rapid precise flow measure; spontaneous inspiratory efforts can invalidate it.


> **Closing point:** A fluid challenge without giving fluid.

items.title: What is the mini fluid challenge?
items.q: What is the mini fluid challenge?
items.a:
- 100 mL over 1 minute.
- A rise in stroke volume or velocity-time integral of 6 to 10% predicts a response.
- Needs a precise flow monitor.
- Reduces the risk of overload compared with a full bolus.


> **Closing point:** Small volume, precise measurement.

items.title: Define fluid responsiveness and distinguish it from hypovolaemia.
items.q: Define fluid responsiveness and distinguish it from hypovolaemia.
items.a:
- Increase in stroke volume of 10 to 15% after a fluid bolus.
- About half of ICU patients and many intraoperative patients respond.
- Responsiveness shows the Starling curve position, not need.
- Consider fluid for hypoperfusion plus responsiveness **and acceptable tolerance**.


> **Closing point:** Responsiveness is a physiological possibility, not an indication.

items.title: How do you assess IVC and what are its limitations?
items.q: How do you assess IVC and what are its limitations?
items.a:
- Measured subcostally, 2 cm from the RA.
- In spontaneous breathing, IVC diameter plus inspiratory change can help estimate RA pressure; strong inspiratory effort can mislead.
- Ventilated-patient distensibility thresholds depend on the formula and strict conditions; IVC variation is not a reliable universal response test.
- Limits: raised intra-abdominal pressure, RV failure, PEEP, arrhythmia.


> **Closing point:** A plethoric IVC suggests a full RA, not a full circulation.

items.title: Give a reproducible structure for a focused cardiac ultrasound assessment.
items.q: Give a reproducible structure for a focused cardiac ultrasound assessment.
items.a:
- LV: size, global/regional function and possible LVOT obstruction.
- RV: size, function and septal position.
- Valves and pericardium: major lesions and tamponade physiology.
- Filling/flow: integrated congestion assessment and measured VTI/SV response.
- Add lung and vascular views for the clinical question.


> **Closing point:** Use a consistent sequence within PG47 scope; no single teaching acronym is an ANZCA-mandated diagnostic algorithm.

Source: Blue Book 2015

items.title: Which TTE views are used in a focused exam?
items.q: Which TTE views are used in a focused exam?
items.a:
- Parasternal long axis.
- Parasternal short axis (papillary muscle level).
- Apical four-chamber.
- Subcostal four-chamber and IVC.
- Add lung views in the shocked patient.


> **Closing point:** Subcostal view works when other windows are poor.

items.title: How do you estimate stroke volume with echo?
items.q: How do you estimate stroke volume with echo?
items.a:
- SV = LVOT area × LVOT velocity-time integral.
- LVOT area = π × (diameter/2)².
- Measure the VTI with pulsed-wave Doppler at the LVOT in the apical five-chamber view.
- Cardiac output = SV × heart rate.
- Error comes from diameter measurement (squared).


> **Closing point:** A change around 10–15% may be useful if acquisition and measurement precision support it.

items.title: What does an underfilled hyperdynamic LV with a small cavity suggest?
items.q: What does an underfilled hyperdynamic LV with a small cavity suggest?
items.a:
- Hypovolaemia or vasodilation.
- Systolic cavity obliteration (kissing papillary muscles).
- Normal or high EF.
- Consider LVOT obstruction.


> **Closing point:** Look at the whole picture, not the EF alone.

items.title: Which findings suggest acute right ventricular strain on echo?
items.q: Which findings suggest acute right ventricular strain on echo?
items.a:
- RV larger than LV (ratio above 1).
- Septal flattening (D-shaped LV) in systole or diastole.
- McConnell sign: RV free-wall hypokinesia with apical sparing; not specific for PE.
- Raised TR velocity, dilated IVC, TAPSE ≤17 mm or S′ ≤9.5 cm/s supports abnormal longitudinal RV function in ASE 2025; integrate other findings.


> **Closing point:** Think pulmonary embolism, RV infarct or acute lung injury.

items.title: What are the echo signs of tamponade?
items.q: What are the echo signs of tamponade?
items.a:
- Pericardial effusion with RA systolic or RV diastolic collapse.
- Plethoric IVC.
- Respiratory variation in mitral and tricuspid inflow.
- Clinical diagnosis: Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus.


> **Closing point:** Ventilation, PH and loculated postoperative collections can obscure classic signs; integrate haemodynamics.

items.title: What is the RUSH or POCUS approach to undifferentiated shock?
items.q: What is the RUSH or POCUS approach to undifferentiated shock?
items.a:
- Pump: LV and RV function, pericardium.
- Tank: IVC, lungs, abdomen (free fluid), pleura.
- Pipes: aorta (aneurysm, dissection), DVT.
- Classifies shock: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive.


> **Closing point:** Pump, tank, pipes.

items.title: Which Doppler formulae do you need to know?
items.q: Which Doppler formulae do you need to know?
items.a:
- Bernoulli: pressure gradient = 4 × V².
- Continuity: A1 × V1 = A2 × V2.
- Aortic valve area from LVOT area and velocity ratio.
- RVSP = 4 × TR velocity² + estimated RA pressure; equals PASP only without pulmonary/RVOT obstruction.


> **Closing point:** Velocity squared times four.

items.title: What are the main limitations of transthoracic echo in anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the main limitations of transthoracic echo in anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Poor windows (obesity, lung disease, ventilated patients, surgical field).
- Operator dependence and training requirement.
- Snapshot rather than continuous.
- Prone/lateral positioning can restrict windows; usable views may still be obtained by a skilled operator.


> **Closing point:** Escalate to TOE when TTE is inadequate.

items.title: When is TOE preferred for haemodynamic monitoring?
items.q: When is TOE preferred for haemodynamic monitoring?
items.a:
- Unstable patient with inadequate TTE windows.
- Repeated imaging of ventricular function, filling/congestion and flow in selected major surgery; not a direct preload-volume measurement.
- Transgastric mid short-axis view monitors ischaemia and filling.
- Perforation/obstructing oesophageal disease/active major GI bleeding are major contraindications; varices, previous surgery and cervical disease require individual assessment.


> **Closing point:** An indwelling TOE probe allows repeated imaging, but interpretation remains intermittent and operator-dependent.

items.title: What makes an arterial pressure system accurate?
items.q: What makes an arterial pressure system accurate?
items.a:
- Adequate natural frequency and damping must be considered together; commonly >20–25 Hz with appropriate damping is desirable, rather than a universal heart-rate multiple.
- Damping coefficient about 0.6 to 0.7.
- Short, stiff tubing without air bubbles.
- Transducer levelled to the right atrium and zeroed to atmosphere.


> **Closing point:** Optimal damping is a compromise between speed and overshoot.

items.title: Under-damped versus over-damped: what do you see?
items.q: Under-damped versus over-damped: what do you see?
items.a:
- Under-damped: overshoot, high systolic, low diastolic, narrow notch.
- Over-damped: low systolic, high diastolic, flattened trace, loss of notch.
- MAP is often less affected, but severe distortion, obstruction or levelling errors can still make it wrong.
- Causes of over-damping: air bubbles, clots, kinks, loose connections.


> **Closing point:** Investigate and correct a poor trace; do not assume its MAP is valid.

items.title: Describe the fast flush test.
items.q: Describe the fast flush test.
items.a:
- Flush briefly and watch the trace.
- Count oscillations after the flush and measure the amplitude ratio.
- One or two oscillations: optimal.
- Many oscillations: under-damped. None: over-damped.


> **Closing point:** Fast flush gives natural frequency and damping.

items.title: What are the complications of radial artery cannulation?
items.q: What are the complications of radial artery cannulation?
items.a:
- Haematoma and bleeding.
- Thrombosis and distal ischaemia (rare).
- Infection.
- Vasospasm and inaccurate readings.
- Nerve injury and arterial injection of drugs.


> **Closing point:** Most radial lines are removed without sequelae.

items.title: What are the problems of non-invasive BP in morbid obesity?
items.q: What are the problems of non-invasive BP in morbid obesity?
items.a:
- Cuff too small gives falsely high readings; too large falsely low.
- Conical arms prevent a good fit.
- Oscillometric devices have errors in obesity.
- Options: forearm or wrist cuff, appropriately sized cuff, invasive arterial line.


> **Closing point:** Cuff bladder should cover 80% of arm circumference.

items.title: Why does peripheral systolic pressure exceed central?
items.q: Why does peripheral systolic pressure exceed central?
items.a:
- Wave reflection and tapering of arteries.
- Systolic higher and diastolic lower distally.
- Mean pressure slightly lower.
- Effect lessens in elderly and with vasodilation.


> **Closing point:** Mean and diastolic pressures vary little.

items.title: Give the formula for oxygen delivery and its normal value.
items.q: Give the formula for oxygen delivery and its normal value.
items.a:
- DO2 = CO × CaO2 × 10 when CO is L/min and CaO2 is mL/dL.
- CaO2 = Hb × 1.34 × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2, with Hb g/dL, saturation as a fraction and PaO2 mmHg; convert NZ g/L/kPa values first.
- Normal about 1000 mL/min (500 to 600 mL/min/m²).
- Consumption about 250 mL/min; extraction ratio 25%.


> **Closing point:** Delivery depends on flow, haemoglobin and saturation.

items.title: What does a high ScvO2 or SvO2 mean?
items.q: What does a high ScvO2 or SvO2 mean?
items.a:
- Reduced extraction (sepsis, mitochondrial dysfunction).
- Shunting or arteriovenous shunt.
- Wedged PA catheter.
- Hypothermia, cyanide, or high oxygen delivery.


> **Closing point:** Normal does not exclude tissue hypoxia.

items.title: List causes of raised lactate.
items.q: List causes of raised lactate.
items.a:
- Type A: tissue hypoxia (shock, regional ischaemia, hypoxaemia, severe anaemia).
- Type B: adrenaline or beta-agonists, liver failure, metformin, thiamine deficiency, malignancy.
- Seizures and exercise.
- Serial change informs assessment; treat the cause, not lactate normalisation with repeated fluid.


> **Closing point:** Interpret lactate with the clinical context.

items.title: What patients benefit from goal-directed therapy?
items.q: What patients benefit from goal-directed therapy?
items.a:
- Consider flow monitoring for selected patients with significant risk, persistent instability or uncertain haemodynamics.
- Match it to the operation, physiology and an actionable treatment question.
- Older pooled benefits are not proof of benefit in every high-risk patient.
- Avoid routine fluid loading or inotrope solely to reach a monitor target.


> **Closing point:** Target the patients who are most at risk.

items.title: What did the OPTIMISE trials show?
items.q: What did the OPTIMISE trials show?
items.a:
- OPTIMISE (2014): cardiac-output-guided protocol, not significant on primary outcome; meta-analysis suggests fewer complications.
- OPTIMISE II (2024): infection 23.2% versus 22.7%; early cardiac events 3.0% versus 1.7% with the tested CO-guided fluid plus routine-inotrope protocol.
- This neutral/harm signal is protocol-specific and does not establish that every flow-monitoring strategy is ineffective.
- Mortality benefit not shown.


> **Closing point:** Verify trial numbers before quoting.

Source: BJA Educ

items.title: What are the capillary refill time findings in sepsis resuscitation?
items.q: What are the capillary refill time findings in sepsis resuscitation?
items.a:
- Normal is under 3 seconds (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK target).
- ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2019: mortality difference was not statistically significant in a superiority trial; it did not prove non-inferiority.
- ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025): personalised CRT-based protocol improved a hierarchical composite (win ratio 1.16), mainly through shorter vital support; not a stand-alone mortality benefit.
- Faster, cheaper and bedside.
- Mottling score adds information.


> **Closing point:** Clinical perfusion indicators are useful targets.

Source: BJA Educ

items.title: What are the principles of fluids in sepsis?
items.q: What are the principles of fluids in sepsis?
items.a:
- Balanced crystalloid first.
- Assess hypoperfusion, responsiveness and tolerance separately; CRT is a perfusion marker, not a responsiveness test.
- Positive balance and high CVP link to harm.
- Noradrenaline for persistent vasoplegia; concurrent fluid/vasopressors may be needed in unstable shock.
- After stabilisation, stop unnecessary inputs and consider monitored diuresis for harmful overload; avoid routine ultrafiltration without an indication.


> **Closing point:** Fluid is a drug with a dose.

Source: BJA Educ 2026

items.title: What determines flow through a cannula?
items.q: What determines flow through a cannula?
items.a:
- Hagen-Poiseuille: flow proportional to radius to the fourth power.
- Inversely proportional to length and viscosity.
- Pressure bag increases the driving pressure.
- Short, wide catheter: highest flow.


> **Closing point:** Halving the radius cuts flow sixteen-fold.

items.title: Give typical flow rates for 14G, 16G and 18G cannulas.
items.q: Give typical flow rates for 14G, 16G and 18G cannulas.
items.a:
- 14G: about 270 mL/min.
- 16G: about 180 mL/min.
- 18G: about 90 mL/min.
- Rapid infusers can exceed 500 mL/min.


> **Closing point:** The colour-coded rates are for water, not blood.

items.title: What are the contraindications to intraosseous access?
items.q: What are the contraindications to intraosseous access?
items.a:
- Fracture or recent IO in that bone.
- Infection at the site.
- Prosthetic joint or surgery at the site.
- Bone disease such as osteogenesis imperfecta requires device/site-specific assessment; use the manufacturer contraindications rather than treating every osteoporosis diagnosis as an absolute ban.


> **Closing point:** Choose another bone if one is not suitable.

items.title: What are the complications of intraosseous access?
items.q: What are the complications of intraosseous access?
items.a:
- Extravasation and compartment syndrome.
- Infection and osteomyelitis.
- Fat embolism and growth plate damage (rare).
- Fracture and failure to position.


> **Closing point:** Replace with suitable definitive access as soon as practical; respect the IO device/local maximum dwell time (often 24 h).

items.title: Which strategies improve peripheral cannulation success?
items.q: Which strategies improve peripheral cannulation success?
items.a:
- Warm the limb, dependent position, tourniquet, hydration.
- Ultrasound guidance.
- Appropriate site and size.
- Experienced operator after two attempts.


> **Closing point:** Plan for the difficult patient.

items.title: How do balanced solutions differ from 0.9% saline?
items.q: How do balanced solutions differ from 0.9% saline?
items.a:
- Saline: sodium 154, chloride 154 mmol/L; strong ion difference zero.
- Balanced solutions have chloride 98 to 110 and a buffer (lactate, acetate, gluconate).
- Large saline volumes cause hyperchloraemic acidosis and possible AKI.
- SMART found a small reduction in a composite kidney outcome; PLUS found no significant 90-day mortality difference. They do not show identical results.


> **Closing point:** Choose balanced crystalloid unless a specific reason exists.

items.title: What is the role of restrictive versus liberal perioperative fluid?
items.q: What is the role of restrictive versus liberal perioperative fluid?
items.a:
- Restrictive and liberal both have harm.
- RELIEF (2018): restrictive regimen did not improve disability-free survival and raised AKI.
- Aim for adequate perfusion without congestion; zero arithmetic balance is not a universal target.
- Use vasopressors rather than fluid for anaesthetic vasodilation.


> **Closing point:** The extremes are worse than the middle.

items.title: What are the harms of synthetic starches?
items.q: What are the harms of synthetic starches?
items.a:
- Increased AKI and renal replacement therapy.
- 6S found increased mortality and RRT in severe sepsis; CHEST found increased RRT without a significant mortality difference.
- Coagulopathy.
- Regulators restrict their use.


> **Closing point:** Avoid hydroxyethyl starch in critically ill patients.

items.title: What are the complication rates by central venous site?
items.q: What are the complication rates by central venous site?
items.a:
- IJ: compressible and accessible to ultrasound; arterial injury/haematoma and pneumothorax remain possible.
- Subclavian/axillary: comfortable with infection/thrombosis advantages in some trials, but bleeding, pleural injury and future dialysis access matter.
- Femoral: useful and compressible; consider retroperitoneal bleeding, thrombosis, hip flexion and site care.
- Rates depend on population, ultrasound, operator, attempts and duration; historical percentages are not universal contemporary risks.


> **Closing point:** Select the site for this patient; there is no universal ranking of total complications.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: How do you prevent vascular injury during IJ cannulation?
items.q: How do you prevent vascular injury during IJ cannulation?
items.a:
- Real-time ultrasound; follow the tip in a competent short-/long-axis or oblique technique.
- Trendelenburg with head rotation below 45 degrees.
- Confirm the wire in the vein by ultrasound before dilating.
- Transduce pressure or check a blood gas before dilation.


> **Closing point:** Check before you dilate.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: How do you manage an inadvertent carotid arterial catheter?
items.q: How do you manage an inadvertent carotid arterial catheter?
items.a:
- Small needle: remove and press for 5 to 10 minutes.
- Large-bore dilator or catheter: do not simply pull.
